items.title: Patrick Criado: “Hay miedo a hablar de nuestras heridas, gente molesta si se muestran otros puntos de vista”
items.description: Decía Pedro Almodóvar que vivir en un pueblo de La Mancha y querer hacer cine era como nacer en Japón y empeñarse en ser torero. Si viniera un matador nipón y pusiera en evidencia a los mejores diestros de España, no sería un caso tan distinto al de Sandra Sánchez, la karateka de Talavera de la Reina (Toledo) que, en 2021, conquistó la medalla de oro en los Juegos Olímpicos de Tokio. “Sandra se enfrentaba no solo al desafío de hacer cada movimiento con la mayor precisión y belleza, sino también a todo un país y su historia”, reflexiona el actor Patrick Criado (Madrid, 31 años), coprotagonista de Karateka, la película sobre la hazaña de la deportista, en cines desde el 30 de octubre. Criado interpreta a Jesús del Moral, entrenador y marido de Sánchez, cuya contribución fue decisiva para que sus cualidades explotaran y llegase a lo más alto a una edad inusual (39 años). Para la Federación Mundial de Kárate, es la mejor karateka en modalidad de kata de todos los tiempos. Seguir leyendo Realización: Nono Vázquez. Asistente de fotografía: Mari Jose Valido. Asistente de realización: Elena Armas. Maquillaje y peluquería: Paúl Gómez (Another Artists).

items.title: El canadiense que fue a la Luna abandera un proyecto urbanístico en Madrid con 12.000 viviendas de lujo: “Va a ser algo extraordinario”
items.description: El canadiense Jeremy Hansen , que en abril se convirtió en la primera persona no estadounidense en viajar hasta la Luna, tiene nuevo trabajo. Este astronauta y piloto de pruebas de 50 años hizo historia como especialista de la misión Artemis 2 , que rodeó el satélite por primera vez en más de 50 años. Seis meses después, Hansen se ha convertido en consejero y embajador de Moon World Resorts, una empresa canadiense que planea construir una enorme réplica de la Luna y un gran complejo turístico, residencial y educativo en torno a una esfera que sería la mayor del mundo. En su interior albergará, según sus promotores, una imitación de la superficie lunar con una colonia visitable. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Carmen Posadas: “Si te llaman fascista entras en ‘shock’, pero es un insulto absurdo”
items.description: Con su minifalda y su forma deshinibida de escribir, Carmen Posadas (Montevideo, 73 años) escandalizó al establishment literario de la España de los ochenta. Igual que las protagonistas de su último libro Las Mitford . Seis hermanas de familia aristocrática y vidas increíbles que rompieron moldes en el Reino Unido de las convenciones. Posadas, sin haber ido a la universidad, se hizo a sí misma. Durante años, no la tomaron en serio. Se habló poco de sus libros y mucho de su relación con Mariano Rubio, entonces gobernador del Banco de España, y de las fiestas a las que acudía. Hoy es libre. Le dan igual los prejuicios y ya no le preocupa el paso del tiempo. Aunque cree que la obsesión por la belleza y la juventud que muestran las redes sociales “ha aumentado la cosificación de las mujeres”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El ‘caso Pérgamo’ llega a su fin: los gestores aceptan devolver la marca a las dueñas de la librería tras registrarla a sus espaldas
items.description: Las letras doradas de la fachada de la librería Pérgamo se quedan en la calle General Oráa. Cuando sus inquilinos anunciaron el pasado 12 de octubre que no les renovaban el alquiler y que se marchaban, todos asumieron que la especulación inmobiliaria había sido la culpable. No era así. Además, en aquel momento publicaron un comunicado en el que aseguraban que Pérgamo no continuaría en la mítica dirección en el madrileño barrio de Salamanca: “Ya estamos trabajando para que la comunidad de Pérgamo pueda seguir creciendo en un nuevo espacio”, se puede leer en sus redes sociales . Tampoco será así. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Cientos de estudiantes de FP en Madrid ven peligrar sus títulos por falta de profesores especialistas
items.description: Cuando Iratxe Correa y Alejandro Castillo pagaron los 400 euros de matrícula para cursar grados superiores de FP en la Comunidad de Madrid, no imaginaron que, por un cambio en el sistema de contratación, no tendrían docentes en asignaturas clave. No son casos aislados: los afectados se cuentan por cientos. Según UGT Madrid, ocurre en el 80% de los centros que necesitan especialistas en las ramas de informática, ingeniería y sanidad. La situación hace que el futuro próximo de estos estudiantes se tambalee: sin la evaluación pertinente, muchos no podrán acceder a la universidad el año que viene, perderán sus notas en la parte específica de la PAU y se quedarán sin becas o las verán reducidas. Educación asegura que está “adoptando todas las medidas necesarias para atender a las necesidades docentes existentes”, que ni detalla ni cuantifica. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La Fiscalía de Cataluña prioriza el derecho al anonimato de un violador impune frente a tres víctimas que piden copia de la investigación
items.description: El Fiscal Superior de Cataluña, Francisco Bañeres, ha denegado el acceso a una investigación reciente sobre un violador en serie a tres de sus víctimas que lo habían solicitado. Tras diversas negativas de Bañeres, una de ellas lo solicitó por escrito el 14 de octubre, tras conocer que se ha obtenido un nuevo perfil genético completo, aunque anónimo, del agresor. Pero dado que los delitos han prescrito, “resulta necesario preservar los derechos fundamentales y los datos personales de terceros”, dice el fiscal en referencia al violador impune cuya identidad podría desvelarse, y añade que la condición de víctima no da “por sí sola, un derecho de acceso” a la investigación. Así consta en un decreto notificado el lunes pasado, dos días después de que EL PAÍS publicase una noticia sobre la falta de respuestas . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los nefrólogos detectan en las consultas un 27% de obesidad oculta: el índice de masa corporal dificulta el acceso al tratamiento
items.description: Obesidad es lo que padece una persona “excesivamente gorda”, según el diccionario de la RAE. Para encuadrarlo en unos parámetros más objetivos, tradicionalmente se ha usado el índice de masa corporal (IMC), que relaciona el peso y la altura. Es un buen detector para la mayoría de la población, pero habitualmente deja fuera a quienes tienen abundante masa muscular o mucha grasa acumulada en la tripa y no en otras zonas. Muchos profesionales llaman a esto último “obesidad oculta” , que padecen casi uno de cada tres pacientes de riñón, según un estudio que se presenta esta semana en el congreso de la Sociedad Española de Nefrología (SEN). Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Andorra cierra filas en torno a Owono, un futbolista roto de dolor que se refugia en su familia
items.description: Un minuto de silencio en memoria de Jesús de Miguel ha marcado este miércoles el regreso a los entrenamientos de los jugadores y del cuerpo técnico del Andorra. La sesión era voluntaria y, con la excusa de estirar las piernas, la suave jornada de trabajo pretendía evitar sobre todo que los miembros de la plantilla se sintieran solos ante la dura carga que arrastran desde la muerte del delantero del Tenerife tras un impactante encontronazo con el portero del club pirenaico. El guardameta, Jesús Owono , ha sido uno de los pocos miembros del equipo que no ha acudido a la cita en el Estadi Comunal, escenario habitual de los entrenamientos del equipo. El club ha decidido protegerlo. Está desconectado en su casa, junto a su pareja y sin teléfono móvil, para aislarlo de las noticias que se suceden sobre el fallecimiento de De Miguel y de la ira generada en las redes sociales. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ablakwa calls for global financial reforms, resource sovereignty
items.description: Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, on Wednesday called on Commonwealth member countries to champion reforms in the global financial architecture to address systemic inequalities confronting developing countries, particularly those in the Global South. He said African countries faced disproportionately high borrowing costs, with access to credit more than eight times as expensive as that available to countries in the Global North, worsening the continent’s debt burden and constraining development. Mr Ablakwa made the call at the Commonwealth Foreign Ministers’ Roundtable in St. John’s Antigua and Barbuda, where he outlined key areas requiring collective action to build a stronger and more responsive Commonwealth. He said the global financial system was structurally skewed against developing economies, with sovereign credit ratings and high-risk premiums contributing to borrowing costs and limiting Africa’s ability to attract investment. Referring to the Highly Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative introduced in 2000, he noted that despite the debt relief achieved, many African countries had returned to similar debt difficulties barely two decades later. He said fundamental reforms were needed to enable African countries to mobilise affordable capital for infrastructure, education, healthcare, industrialisation and job creation. Mr Ablakwa said Africa’s youthful population, with a median age of 19, underscored the urgency of creating sustainable economic opportunities for young people. He expressed Ghana’s support for the Bridgetown Initiative, championed by Barbados, and urged the Commonwealth to prioritise proposals to reform the international financial system and improve access to development financing. The Minister also called for greater resource sovereignty, urging African countries to move beyond extracting and exporting raw materials towards local value addition and industrialisation. He cited President John Dramani Mahama’s Accra Reset Initiative, which seeks to promote greater African ownership of natural resources and ensure that their exploitation directly benefits local populations. Mr Ablakwa said growing global demand for critical minerals, particularly those needed for artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies, presented significant opportunities for Africa but also carried risks. He cautioned against partnerships that prioritised access to the continent’s resources without guaranteeing commensurate benefits, warning that such arrangements could perpetuate historical patterns of exploitation. He said engagements with international partners, particularly within the Commonwealth, should promote local processing, technology transfer, industrialisation and employment creation. “We no longer want to just be looting grounds, to be very blunt, where natural resources are just extracted. We want to add value,” he said. Mr Ablakwa said industrialisation and the creation of decent jobs were also essential to addressing irregular migration, particularly the dangerous journeys undertaken by young Africans across the Mediterranean in search of better livelihoods. On governance, he urged Commonwealth countries to prioritise local government reforms in response to the challenges of rapid urbanisation. He said Ghana was undertaking constitutional reforms to ensure that local government officials were elected rather than appointed, to deepen democracy and strengthen grassroots participation. The proposed reforms, he said, would give citizens greater influence over decisions affecting their communities, including the management of local resources. He encouraged Commonwealth member states to share experiences and best practices in decentralisation and local governance to improve democratic accountability and development outcomes. Mr Ablakwa cautioned against decentralisation arrangements that left local authorities effectively controlled by central governments through appointments, saying such systems denied communities meaningful participation in decisions affecting their development. He also commended the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association for supporting Ghana in capacity building, strengthening parliamentary institutions and promoting the fight against corruption. He said the Association’s continued partnership had contributed to strengthening Ghana’s democratic institutions. Mr Ablakwa, who is also a Member of Ghana’s Parliament, reaffirmed Ghana’s commitment to working with Commonwealth partners to advance shared development priorities through equitable partnerships, democratic governance and mutual respect.

items.title: Shafay ‘distances’ himself from Salik
items.description: LAHORE: Punjab Commerce and Investment Minister Shafay Hussain has apparently distanced himself from his younger brother Salik Hussain, Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis who levelled corruption allegations against the provincial government of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz a few days ago. Shafay’s unequivocal support for Maryam has reportedly saved his position in the Punjab cabinet. “Shafay Hussain’s recent interviews have been supportive of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, so we have no plan to denotify him from the Punjab cabinet,” Information and Culture Minister Azma Bokhari told Dawn on Wednesday when asked whether the provincial government was considering removing him following his younger brother’s outburst against the chief minister. “Shafay Hussain has rejected Salik’s allegations,” she added. The PML-Q has only one minister in the Punjab cabinet — Shafay Hussain. On Tuesday, Ms Nawaz served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Salik over his corruption allegations against her government, demanding that he retract his remarks. Salik said on Wednesday that he would respond to the notice. Azma says no plan to denotify elder brother The controversy also drew in former Punjab chief minister Chaudhry Parvez Elahi’s son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, who took a swipe at Ms Nawaz over her remarks about Gujrat in a post on X. “Punjab was not handed over to you by my father. In fact, you became chief minister because of Form-47,” he said. Meanwhile, Ms Bokhari asked Mr Salik to substantiate his corruption allegations or apologise, saying he could not enjoy the privileges of being part of the government while simultaneously engaging in political mudslinging. She said it was unbecoming of a federal minister and a member of the ruling coalition to level allegations without producing evidence. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif also weighed in on the controversy through a post on X, saying Mr Salik’s remarks about corruption in Punjab were beyond his limited political understanding. “Corruption is one of the biggest challenges facing our society, and it is the collective responsibility of the entire political leadership, both at the federal and provincial levels, to rid the country of this menace.” The PML-Q is part of both the federal and provincial governments. We should join hands and wage a collective war against corruption,” he said. Asif further said if Salik’s statement is part of a future political agenda aimed at targeting Ms Nawaz’s government to carve out political space for himself at both the provincial and federal levels and secure his political future, “it would make sense.” The latest exchange comes against the backdrop of a political split within the Chaudhry family following the ouster of Imran Khan’s government through a no-confidence vote in 2022. While Chaudhry Parvez Elahi and his son Moonis Elahi aligned themselves with the PTI, Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain’s sons, Salik and Shafay, chose to side with the Sharifs. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: US midterms: World leaders hope for reset
items.description: PARIS: World leaders voiced hopes for a reset with the United States on Wednesday after voters delivered a huge midterm election defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican party. Germany German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he hoped to see new initiatives to end the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. “With their majority in both chambers of Congress, the De­­m­­ocratic Party will likely seek to shift the political course in the United States,” Wadephul said. Through cooperation betwe­­en the United States and Eur­ope, “there may be a new oppo­r­­­t­­unity to launch a fresh initiative” to resolve conflicts, he said. Spain Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Trump’s defeat showed that the global far-right was on the wane. “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain,” the socialist leader said, with elections looming later this month. The far-right wave is “no longer growing, it is unravelling,” he added. Russia Russia hopes Trump will continue his “peacemaking efforts” after the midterm elections, the Kremlin said. “President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will also continue his peacemaking effo­r­­ts,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. South Africa South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the result could thaw strained ties between Pretoria and Washington. “We’re hoping that on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters,” he said. He added that he hoped the result would “introduce a new era in world relations”. EU The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas voiced hope the new US Congress would support Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia. “I hope that the new Congress… will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia,” she said, adding that Europe and the United States “are much stronger together” in pushing Moscow to end its war. UK UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the result was an opportunity for the world to “unite” around resolving cost-of-living issues. “President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living,” Burnham said. items.title: FC Barcelone : blessé, Rodri forfait contre l’Atlético de Madrid et avec la Roja
items.description: Le milieu de terrain du FC Barcelone, Rodrigo Hernández « Rodri », sera forfait pour le déplacement du club catalan à l’Atlético de Madrid, dimanche, en Liga, en raison d’une « petite blessure » au biceps fémoral de la cuisse droite, a annoncé mercredi le club blaugrana. Le joueur a passé des examens médicaux après avoir ressenti une gêne musculaire lors de la victoire du FC Barcelone face à Aston Villa (3-0), mardi, en Ligue des champions. Il avait été remplacé à la mi-temps par Marc Bernal. « Les examens ont confirmé une petite blessure au biceps fémoral de la cuisse droite. Il sera absent du match de dimanche contre l’Atlético de Madrid. La durée exacte de sa convalescence dépendra de l’évolution de la blessure », a précisé le FC Barcelone dans son communiqué. Cette indisponibilité privera également la sélection espagnole de son milieu, qui manquera les deux dernières rencontres de la phase de groupes de la Ligue des nations, face à la Tchéquie, le 12 novembre à Prague, puis à l’Angleterre, le 15 novembre. Le sélectionneur Luis de la Fuente doit dévoiler vendredi la liste des joueurs convoqués pour ces deux rencontres. Cette indisponibilité s'ajoute à une infirmerie catalane déjà bien garnie, comptant notamment les défenseurs Jules Koundé, Eric García, Xavi Espart et Andreas Christensen, le milieu offensif Dani Olmo, ainsi que l'attaquant Roony Bardghji, blessé de longue date. items.title: TraffiTech-GH: ‘If fines are too expensive, don’t overspeed’ – Mahama to motorists
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has told motorists unhappy with the penalties under the newly introduced TraffiTech-GH traffic enforcement system to avoid speeding rather than complain about the cost of fines. He said drivers who observed prescribed speed limits would have no reason to worry about penalties, insisting that compliance with traffic regulations was the straightforward way to avoid sanctions. “If it [fines] is too expensive, then don’t overspend; that’s all, there is a solution to it,” the President said. Mr Mahama made the remarks in an interview with 1957 News on the sidelines of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) at Jumby Bay Island in Antigua and Barbuda, where he discussed the introduction of the automated traffic monitoring system and concerns surrounding its implementation. His comments come amid public debate over the level of fines imposed under TraffiTech-GH, with some motorists questioning whether the penalties are proportionate, particularly given the condition of roads in parts of the country. Compliance, not complaints The president maintained that the enforcement of speed limits was necessary to address dangerous driving and reduce preventable road crashes. He rejected suggestions that the government should postpone the deployment of the technology until roads and related infrastructure had been fully improved. According to him, road repairs and traffic law enforcement should proceed together, since the condition of the country’s roads does not justify allowing motorists to exceed speed limits. He cited the use of speed cameras in the United Kingdom, arguing that traffic enforcement technology was deployed there even though its road network was not without imperfections. “My understanding is that Traffitech has begun with overspeeding; they have not yet added the other components of jumping red light, parking wrongly,” he said. “And so I hear they [the public] say we should fix the roads before we introduce Traffitech. I mean, it doesn’t happen like that. The roads are not perfect in the UK, and yet they have speed cameras,” he added. Speed cameras to carry warning signs Despite defending the system, President Mahama has directed the police and agencies responsible for its implementation to install clear warning signs ahead of locations where speed cameras are deployed. He said motorists should be informed when approaching monitored sections of the road, describing public notification as an important part of introducing technology-driven traffic enforcement. “All I will urge is that the police and those implementing Traffitech should put signs showing where the cameras are, because that is one of the things you need to do if you are introducing this kind of innovation,” he said. “You need to put signposts, warning motorists, that there is a speed camera ahead. I think that transparency is important,” he added. The directive is intended to ensure that motorists are not taken by surprise by the monitoring system and are adequately informed about its operation. Road safety at the centre of the debate President Mahama also defended the need for stricter speed enforcement, pointing to the danger posed by speeding vehicles to pedestrians, particularly schoolchildren. He said children returning from school were frequently knocked down by vehicles, with some losing their lives while others suffered injuries that left them permanently disabled. “If you look at the number of children knocked down every year in Ghana when they are coming from school, you will understand why it is important for us to check over speeding. Children coming from school are knocked down and killed or permanently injured, and so it is important for us to check speeding,” he said. The TraffiTech-GH system has initially focused on detecting speeding, with other traffic violations, including running red lights and illegal parking, expected to be incorporated into the wider enforcement framework. The initiative forms part of efforts to strengthen compliance with road traffic regulations through technology and improve road safety. While the President has acknowledged the need for transparency in the deployment of the cameras, his message to motorists concerned about the cost of penalties remains that observing speed limits is the surest way to avoid them.

items.title: How Absa is connecting affluent banking with lifestyle experiences
items.description: As customer expectations evolve, premium banking in Ghana is increasingly extending beyond traditional financial services. While access to credit, investment solutions, and everyday banking services remain important, many affluent customers also seek convenience, access, and experiences that complement their lifestyles. This shift is reflected in how banks worldwide are redefining their premium banking propositions. Payment cards that once served primarily as transaction tools are increasingly being positioned as gateways to travel, entertainment, dining and other lifestyle benefits for affluent customers. Global premium card programmes now place significant emphasis on experiences, concierge support and exclusive access privileges alongside traditional banking services. The trend mirrors broader changes in consumer behaviour. A 2024 Mastercard study of affluent consumers across 23 markets found that experiences such as travel, entertainment, and dining are becoming increasingly important priorities, with 59% of affluent consumers preferring to spend on experiences rather than acquire additional material possessions. The study also found that travel ranks among the leading personal aspirations for many affluent consumers. As customer priorities change, banks are rethinking how they create value and build loyalty. Research suggests that traditional card rewards based solely on points, discounts, and cashback are giving way to more personalised approaches that focus on customer engagement and experiences. The report notes that banks are increasingly seeking ways to strengthen customer relationships beyond the transaction itself. For Absa Bank Ghana, this evolution is reflected in the proposition attached to its Signature and Infinite Cards. Beyond facilitating payments, the cards offer a range of benefits designed to support customers across different aspects of their personal and professional lives. Benefits available through the Absa Signature and Infinite Card propositions include access to more than 1,200 airport lounges worldwide, concierge services, multi-trip international travel insurance and discounts through selected partner institutions. Together, these benefits are intended to provide greater convenience and flexibility for customers who travel frequently, conduct business internationally or seek premium travel and lifestyle experiences.Charles Addo, Director of Personal and Private Banking at Absa Bank Ghana, says changing expectations among affluent customers are shaping how banks think about customer value. “Banking today is about much more than facilitating transactions. Affluent customers want solutions that fit seamlessly into their lives and deliver value in the moments that matter most. That includes travel, lifestyle, convenience and access. Our Signature and Infinite Cards are designed with those expectations in mind, and initiatives such as the Champagne in Africa experience are one way of bringing that proposition to life for our customers.” One example is the Bank’s ongoing engagement with the Champagne in Africa Festival, a premium lifestyle event that celebrates French champagne alongside African fashion, art, food and music. Through successive editions of the campaign, Absa has linked its premium card proposition to experiential rewards, giving eligible Signature and Infinite Card customers the opportunity to attend the festival based on their card usage. The approach continues in 2026, with Ghanaian Signature or Infinite Card customers earning the opportunity to attend this year’s Champagne in Africa Festival in Johannesburg, South Africa, by participating in the campaign. For banks serving affluent customers, the challenge is remaining relevant in a competitive environment where products and pricing alone may not be enough to maintain customer loyalty. Travel benefits, lifestyle experiences, access and convenience are becoming important differentiators, helping institutions build stronger customer relationships and create value beyond traditional banking interactions. As affluent banking evolves, the distinction between financial services and lifestyle experiences is becoming less pronounced. Institutions that succeed will likely be those that understand not only their customers’ financial needs but also the aspirations, interests, and experiences that shape how they live, work, and travel.

items.title: Telecel champions inclusivity at Disability Inclusive Hackathon 2026
items.description: Telecel Ghana participated in this year’s Disability Inclusive Hackathon (DI-HACKATHON), organised by the Inclusive Tech Group and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Ghana Section as part of its 10 th International Conference on Adaptive Science and Technology (ICAST) celebration. Held at the Academic City University in Accra, the event ran under the theme “Engineering a Resilient Future through Convergent Technologies.” DI-HACKATHON is the Inclusive Tech Group’s flagship annual initiative to spark rapid, collaborative innovation in assistive technology. Software developers, engineers, UI/UX designers, and disability advocates co-create practical solutions to real-world accessibility challenges. People living with disabilities join the teams to develop technologies such as sensory navigation aids and inclusive educational software built for the communities they serve. Alongside PwC and Google, Telecel Ghana was a main sponsor and contributed through employee participation in mentoring and judging. Anna Owooson, In-Market Delivery Lead, and Johnson Oteng-Dartey, Technical BI Developer from Telecel, mentored teams throughout the competition, guiding them as they refined concepts and built prototypes. On the judging panel, Dr Joyce Koi-Akrofi, Capital Programmes Manager, Telecel, and Mr Asiedu Ansu, Head of Data & Analytics Centre of Excellence, Telecel, joined other industry experts to evaluate the solutions, underscoring Telecel’s commitment to innovation that advances accessibility and inclusion. Telecel mentored projects including software to help people with dexterity impairments navigate online platforms; an image-based communication tool for people with speech or hearing impairments during medical consultations; and a wearable device that alerts deaf individuals to sounds such as a doorbell or a crying child. Anna Owooson, speaking on her experience as a mentor, said, “Mentoring these young innovators was rewarding, and every idea was impressive. The highlight was when one of my projects won. I also drew on Telecel’s digital specialists for guidance on certain challenges. The hackathon gave these young engineers the chance to build solutions for the disability community while working alongside people with specific impairments. It was a truly remarkable opportunity.” This initiative is part of Telecel’s disability-focused programmes for October, observed internally as Care and Wellbeing Month. Telecel also partnered with the Ghana National Association for the Deaf to commemorate the International Week of the Deaf and hosted STEM training for 100 persons with disabilities in Hohoe, Volta Region. Telecel Ghana consistently champions disability inclusion through mobile technology, specialised customer service, and technical education for the deaf, blind, and speech-impaired communities. It employs 10 deaf professionals and serves over 3,500 members of the Deaf community through heavily discounted voice and data offerings, dedicated support channels, and accessible platforms, including the Telecel Play App and *494#.

items.title: ‘He’s innocent until proven guilty’ – Agalga says Parliament united on Kwame Frimpong’s rights
items.description: Majority Leader James Agalga says Parliament is united on protecting detained Asante Akyem North MP Ohene Kwame Frimpong’s rights, insisting he must be presumed innocent. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, Agalga rejected suggestions that Parliament could declare the MP’s seat vacant while he faces extradition proceedings in the Netherlands. “He’s innocent until proven guilty. Then there’s unanimity in Parliament that we must respect that principle.” Asked whether Frimpong’s seat would be declared vacant, he was emphatic. “No, we can’t do that. He’s not been convicted. If you declare the seat vacant and the courts clear him, what happens?” Agalga said Parliament had a duty to respect its colleague’s rights throughout the proceedings. “Yes, we have to respect his rights. To do otherwise would violate his rights. His right to innocence, the presumption of innocence, is well enshrined in our constitution.” Frimpong was arrested at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport on May 10, 2026, after arriving from Ghana. His detention followed a US extradition request linked to allegations of romance scams and money laundering. He remains in Dutch custody after an initial bail application and an appeal failed. His extradition hearing is scheduled for November 18, 2026, according to Majority Chief Whip Rockson-Nelson Dafeamekpor. Parliament has engaged Ghana’s mission in The Hague, and Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has confirmed consular support, including a visit to the detainee. Agalga said he had received a formal briefing. However, he acknowledged that he did not know the precise details of the alleged scam. “I do not know the actual details. In fact, when the pressures of work ease a bit, I intend to pay him a visit.” He said the visit would help him obtain firsthand information about the case. Asked about official support, Agalga said Ghana’s mission in Brussels was assisting the MP and had been supportive. He welcomed that intervention. “For me, that is a step in the right direction. So we wish our colleague well.”

items.title: Too many schoolchildren dying on our roads – Mahama backs TraffiTech
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has defended the introduction of the TraffiTech-GH speed enforcement system, citing the deaths and life-changing injuries suffered by schoolchildren knocked down by speeding vehicles as a compelling reason for stricter traffic regulation. He said the country could no longer afford to delay measures to control speeding while children continued to lose their lives or sustain permanent disabilities on their way home from school. The president said protecting vulnerable road users, particularly schoolchildren, must be a priority in the country’s efforts to reduce road crashes. “If you look at the number of children knocked down every year in Ghana when they are coming from school, you will understand why it is important for us to check over speeding. Children coming from school are knocked down and killed or permanently injured, and so it is important for us to check speeding,” he said. Speaking to 1957 New s on the sidelines of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) at Jumby Bay Island in Antigua and Barbuda, President Mahama maintained that the need to protect lives justified the deployment of technology to enforce traffic regulations. His comments come amid public debate over the introduction of TraffiTech-GH, particularly concerns about the cost of penalties, the condition of roads and whether motorists should be subjected to stricter enforcement before the government addresses existing infrastructure deficiencies. Road safety cannot wait. President Mahama rejected arguments that the government should first repair roads and improve related infrastructure before introducing the automated traffic enforcement system. He said road maintenance and traffic law enforcement were not mutually exclusive responsibilities and that deficiencies in the road network should not become an excuse for allowing dangerous driving to continue. He cited the United Kingdom, where speed cameras are deployed despite roads not being in perfect condition, to support his argument that traffic enforcement should not be postponed until all infrastructure challenges have been resolved. “My understanding is that Traffitech has begun with overspeeding; they have not yet added the other components of jumping red lights and parking wrongly. And so I hear they [the public] say we should fix the roads before we introduce Traffitech. I mean, it doesn’t happen like that. The roads are not perfect in the UK, and yet they have speed cameras,” he said. The President’s argument is that controlling excessive speed is an immediate road safety intervention, particularly in areas where pedestrians and children are exposed to fast-moving vehicles. Road crash figures reinforce concerns Available road safety statistics highlight the scale of the country’s road safety challenge. Figures released by the National Road Safety Authority (NRSA) show that Ghana recorded 2,949 road crash deaths in 2025, compared with 2,494 in 2024, representing an 18.2 per cent increase. The crashes also resulted in 16,714 injuries, while pedestrian knockdowns increased by seven per cent to 2,561 cases. Of those killed in road crashes during 2025, 328 were below 18 years, representing approximately 11 per cent of the fatalities. The figures underline the risks faced by children and other vulnerable road users, although the national statistics do not separately establish how many of the child fatalities occurred while pupils were travelling to or from school. The NRSA has repeatedly called for stronger enforcement and greater cooperation among road safety stakeholders to reverse the rising fatalities. Warning signs for motorists While defending the speed enforcement initiative, President Mahama said its implementation must be transparent, with motorists adequately informed about the locations of the cameras. He specifically urged the police and the agencies responsible for TraffiTech-GH to install visible signposts ahead of camera locations to alert drivers that they were approaching monitored sections of the road. He said advance notification would help motorists understand where the technology was deployed and encourage compliance with speed limits. “All I will urge is that the police and those implementing Traffitech should put up signs showing where the cameras are, because that is one of the things you need to do if you are introducing this kind of innovation. You need to put signposts, warning motorists, that there is a speed camera ahead. I think that transparency is important,” he said. The directive, he indicated, was intended to ensure that the introduction of technology-driven enforcement was accompanied by openness and adequate public information. ‘Don’t overspeed’ On complaints that the fines imposed under the TraffiTech-GH system were too high, the president urged motorists to avoid the penalties by observing prescribed speed limits. He maintained that drivers who complied with traffic regulations would have no reason to incur speeding fines. “If it is too expensive, then don’t overspeed; that’s all, there is a solution to it,” he said. The TraffiTech-GH system is expected to strengthen enforcement of road traffic regulations through automated monitoring, with speeding enforcement forming the initial phase. Other violations, including running red lights and illegal parking, are also envisaged under the broader system. President Mahama’s defence of the initiative places the protection of schoolchildren and other vulnerable road users at the centre of the debate, as the government seeks to use technology to address dangerous driving and reduce preventable deaths on Ghana’s roads.

items.title: NAB summons Fazl’s son in Pakistan Post case
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) has summoned former federal minister for communication Asad Mahmood, who is the son of JUI-F president Maulana Fazlur Rehman, for alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments at Pakistan Post during his 2022-23 term. The development came after Maulana Fazl’s new tirade against the government and state institutions on issues concerning main opposition Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) and terrorism. According to a NAB notice, the bureau is investigating alleged irregularities in appointments made at Pakistan Post during Mr Mahmood’s tenure as federal minister between 2022 and 2023. The ex-minister is accused of making as many as 4,252 appointments against fewer approved vacancies, with discrepancies in the number of sanctioned posts in Pakistan Post. The anti-graft watchdog has directed Mr Mahmood to appear before its investigation team on Nov 10 at 11am. Bureau to probe excessive appointments allegedly in violation of cabinet committee’s direction Mr Mahmood had served as federal minister during the last PML-N-led Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM) government in 2022-23. The PDM had formed the government after toppling the Imran Khan government, which had served from 2018 to 2022, through a vote of no-confidence. The notice stated that the Establishment Division had authorised recruitment against 3,938 posts at Pakistan Post. However, 4,252 people were allegedly appointed, exceeding the approved number. The NAB said that 2,646 appointments were made against posts that had already been abolished, in violation of the directions of a cabinet committee. The bureau said a large number of permanent appointments were made against the recommendation for recruitment on a contractual basis only. The investigation also covered allegations that the appointments placed an additional financial burden on Pakistan Post. The aspect of alleged political affiliations among some selected candidates is also being examined. Other allegations include the use of fake and forged documents, recruitment of candidates over the prescribed age limit and violations of the domicile quota during the hiring process. The NAB has warned that failure to comply with the summons could result in legal action under Section 31 of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999. FIA probe The notice by NAB has been issued at a time when the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) is also investigating alleged corruption and irregularities in Pakistan Post recruitments. The FIA’s Anti-Corruption Circle in Islamabad had separately issued a notice summoning Mr Mahmood to record his statement in connection with the case. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

Then there’s unanimity in Parliament that we must respect that principle.” Mr Frimpong was arrested at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport on May 10, 2026, after arriving from Ghana, following a US extradition request. Parliament confirmed his detention and contacted Ghana’s diplomatic mission in The Hague. Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa subsequently confirmed consular assistance, including a visit to the MP. Two attempts to secure bail have failed. Majority Chief Whip Rockson-Nelson Dafeamekpor has said the extradition hearing is scheduled for November 18, 2026. Mr Agalga confirmed that he had been formally briefed. However, he said he did not know the precise details of the alleged scam. “I do not know the actual details. In fact, when the pressures of work ease a bit, I intend to pay him a visit.” He said the planned visit would help him obtain firsthand information about the case. The Majority Leader also said Ghana’s mission in Brussels was assisting the detained legislator. “He’s a Member of Parliament, so our mission in Brussels is assisting.” For now, he said, Parliament was awaiting the outcome of the court applications. “We pray for our colleague that the applications that are currently before the court would come out favourably for him”.

items.title: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
items.description: A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was “unethical” and “neocolonial”. The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines. Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy. The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns. Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries. The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment. Here is what you need to know. What was the trial? The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978. It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot . Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection. Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality. Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028. But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world’s poorest countries, where the infection is widespread. The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025 . What did the WHO say? Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol. He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B. “The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries,” he said. “A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical.” He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life. Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver. Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020. The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine. “The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year,” Mulombo said. Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective. Why did Guinea-Bissau reject the trial? Guinea-Bissau’s government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all. “We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed,” Nantote said. “We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed.” The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval “from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau,” which Nantote denied. Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal. “The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism,” he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark. His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread. SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research. Was the trial approved by anyone? The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university’s own research ethics committee. Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one. He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review. Following the approval from the SDU’s ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed. He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau’s authorities. What has happened to the vaccines? On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau’s Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project’s facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines. Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation. They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe. The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch. Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines. Who is funding the research? The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy. Under Kennedy’s leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration. Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study’s stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection. Kennedy has praised the Danish researchersas “the deities of vaccine research”, and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect. There is no evidence in the information available that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.

He termed the performance of the Directorate General of Immigration and Passports and its efforts towards institutional reforms commendable, emphasising the need to further modernise the system in line with contemporary requirements. Mr Nasar said the use of modern technology, digital systems and automation should be expanded at all stages of passport issuance to make the entire process, from submission of an application to passport delivery, faster, more transparent and accessible. He emphasised that citizens should not face unnecessary delays, prolonged waiting periods or administrative complications, adding that an effective mechanism must be ensured for the prompt resolution of complaints. “Effective use of modern technology and improved administrative strategies could further strengthen public confidence in the institution,” Mr Nasar added. items.title: Smart farming, weak connections: Rethinking rural connectivity in Ghana
items.description: Farming involves a succession of decisions. Is the soil dry enough to need watering? Has a grazing animal wandered too far? Is a change in its behaviour a sign that something is wrong? Farmers have always relied on observation and experience to answer such questions. Digital tools extend what they can see, measure, and act on. A small electronic sensor can measure moisture beneath the soil surface. A collar can record an animal’s location or activity. A controller connected to an irrigation valve can turn water on when it is needed. These are some of the ideas behind smart agriculture: using measurements to guide decisions and, sometimes, letting equipment act automatically. For these tools to work together, information must travel. A reading must reach the farmer or a controller; an instruction must reach a pump; an alert must reach someone who can respond. The communications network provides those connections. Its design can determine whether useful equipment becomes part of everyday farming or remains an impressive demonstration. Ghana’s discussion of agricultural modernisation needs to pay more attention to that network. Buying sensors and developing applications are only part of the investment. Connecting them across fields, grazing areas, and scattered settlements is a challenge in itself. Ghana is already exploring the possibilities Local initiatives offer a starting point. KNUST’s DIPPER Lab, Sesi Technologies and Manchester Metropolitan University have collaborated on FarmSense. KNUST reported launching its soil sensor in October 2025, measuring soil moisture, temperature, and acidity. Such information can help farmers and agricultural advisers understand conditions that are difficult to judge from the surface alone. Livestock offers another example. DIPPER Lab’s HerdWatch, also described as Aurok-1, uses a wearable collar to collect location, activity and other measurements relevant to animal health. The laboratory describes a prototype ready for field testing, with data sent through an LTE mobile connection to an online platform. It is intended to help farmers locate cattle and recognise signs that an animal may need attention. KNUST’s Responsible Artificial Intelligence Lab also identifies crop water requirements and automated irrigation as part of its agricultural research directions. Together, these initiatives show that the discussion extends from crop production to livestock management and equipment control. They represent different stages of development, rather than evidence that connected farming is already widely established. Their broader relevance raises a practical question: what connections will farmers need for tools like these to become dependable services? A soil test recorded on a phone may be useful without continuous internet access. Remotely following a moving herd or receiving timely alerts presents a different challenge. What data needs to travel across the farm Consider an illustrative cooperative growing vegetables and keeping livestock across several dispersed sites. Its members want better irrigation decisions, help locating cattle and a way to send photographs of damaged crops to an extension officer. Each task asks something different of the network. A moisture sensor may send only a short reading at intervals. The message is small, and the device may need to run for months on a battery. Transmitting continuously would waste energy. A photograph contains far more information, so the connection needs greater capacity: the ability to carry more data in a given time. An animal collar adds movement to the problem. GPS can help the device determine the animal’s location, but that position still needs a separate communication link to reach the farmer. A location shown on yesterday’s map offers little help when cattle have moved beyond the network’s service area. Health monitoring introduces urgency. Changes in temperature or activity could trigger an alert for inspection; they do not by themselves establish a diagnosis. The useful service is one that gets a meaningful warning to the farmer or animal-health worker soon enough to investigate. Automation goes a step further. A sensor provides information; an automated system uses information and agreed rules to operate equipment. An irrigation controller might open a valve when the soil becomes too dry, then close it after a set limit. That action needs safeguards, including a way for the farmer to intervene. This is why a farm network should be planned around the work. Key questions include how much information must move, how quickly it must arrive, where devices will operate, and how long their batteries must last. The internet is not always required The cooperative would need to distinguish connections within its farms from connections to services elsewhere. Nearby sensors can send readings to a local controller or gateway, a device that gathers messages and forwards them. The onward connection to the wider internet is often called backhaul. A local controller can keep irrigation operating during an internet interruption, using stored rules and safe limits. Records can be uploaded when the external connection returns. Remote advice, off-site supervision and shared records still benefit from internet access, but essential farm operations should have a sensible response when it fails. This distinction can also reduce costs. A short sensor message does not need the same connection as a large image upload. Some decisions can be made close to the equipment, leaving the onward link to carry information that genuinely needs to travel further. Connecting scattered farms can be commercially challenging. A provider must pay for equipment, power, transmission links and maintenance, then recover those costs from users spread over a wide area. Demand may be modest or seasonal. These conditions can weaken the investment case for conventional mobile expansion. The problem varies by location. Some farms already have useful cellular coverage, and a service available in a village may perform differently across surrounding fields. The first step is to measure what is available where the equipment will actually work. Where existing services fall short, the cooperative might aggregate demand and purchase a shared connection from a qualified provider. A processor, irrigation scheme or nearby institution could also contribute demand. Sharing gives more users a way to support the fixed costs, although it still requires dependable payments and clear responsibility for repairs. Where television white spaces could help Wireless systems communicate using radio frequencies. The range of frequencies available for different services is known as radio spectrum. Television broadcasting uses part of that spectrum, but the channels protected services occupy vary by location. Subject to regulatory permission, some locally available channels can carry data. These are television white spaces, or TVWS. Their appeal for agriculture lies partly in how these radio signals travel. Compared with higher-frequency links under comparable conditions, they can offer advantages over distance and around some obstacles. That could help connect dispersed farm sites with fewer intermediate installations. Actual performance still depends on terrain, vegetation, antennas and permitted power. For our illustrative cooperative, TVWS could carry information between farm clusters and a central point with internet access. Small sensors would use suitable local links to a gateway; they would not each need a specialised TVWS radio. Fibre, cellular service or satellite could provide the onward internet connection. The FarmBeats research project provides a precedent for combining TVWS links between farm base stations and an internet gateway with local Wi-Fi connections. Its experience on United States farms offers an architectural example to examine, rather than a ready-made cost model for Ghana. TVWS also has limits. A shared link must accommodate all its users, and large image transfers can compete with other traffic. Equipment availability and technical support matter. Before selecting a technology, compare cellular service, other wireless options, and satellite for the same farming tasks. Sharing spectrum requires careful listening (sensing) Because broadcasters must remain protected, identifying usable channels is essential. Lydia Kyeraa’s MPhil research at KNUST examines one part of this problem: cooperative spectrum sensing. Sensing means listening for evidence that a radio channel is occupied. Cooperation combines observations from several receivers, rather than relying on a single listening point. A weak broadcast signal may be obscured at one receiver by local conditions or background noise. Combining observations can help the system make better judgments. Mistaking an occupied channel for an available one risks interference; mistakenly rejecting an available channel wastes a communication opportunity. Lydia’s work investigates detection methods through simulation, including machine-learning approaches. It contributes to understanding spectrum sharing; it has not demonstrated an agricultural network in the field or established savings for farmers. Testing on real equipment would need to examine accuracy, energy use and processing demands. Ghana’s published NCA TVWS guidelines require location-based access to an approved database to establish usable channels and power levels. Listening alone does not grant permission to transmit. The guidelines also provide for regulatory fees. Any proposed deployment should therefore confirm current approvals, charges and database arrangements with the NCA. Build a service that survives the demonstration The cooperative’s final decision would depend on the complete service cost: radios, installation, electricity or solar power, batteries, internet access and maintenance. A network described as inexpensive at purchase can become costly if faults require repeated specialist visits. Seasonal incomes also matter when bills run year-round. A useful pilot should begin with a farming decision that participants value, such as scheduling irrigation or locating animals. It should test whether information arrives when needed, whether equipment behaves sensibly during outages and whether farmers can obtain support. Agricultural specialists should assess whether the information actually improves practice, while network specialists compare feasible connections under the same conditions. Trials should run through relevant seasons and operating conditions. They should establish who owns the equipment, who protects access to farm data and controls, who repairs failures and how replacement parts will be paid for. Expansion should follow evidence that both the agricultural application and the service model work. Ghana has researchers and enterprises developing tools for more informed farming. Connecting those tools deserves the same practical attention as building them. For the farmer, the value is water applied at the right time, an animal found sooner, or a warning investigated before a problem grows. The network earns its place when it makes those outcomes dependable.

items.title: Morocco says it will uphold Western Sahara ceasefire after UN mission ends
items.description: Morocco will remain committed to the ceasefire in Western Sahara even after the United Nations peacekeeping mission in the territory ends, the Royal Palace said on Wednesday. The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission came to an end after the ‌Security Council did not renew its mandate last week, the UN said on Sunday, removing the international presence that has monitored the ceasefire in the decades-old dispute. The Western Sahara conflict pits Morocco, which considers the ​territory its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, a political and military organisation ​that has been seeking a separate state there since the departure of ⁠former colonial power Spain in 1976. Morocco’s “voluntary commitment” to the ceasefire will not change with ​the end of the UN mission, the palace said in a statement, following a meeting ​chaired by King Mohammed VI with the prime minister, royal adviser, and the army chief. Morocco expressed satisfaction at the non-renewal of the mission, the Polisario said it was “concerned” and Algeria expressed “deep regret.” Morocco controls all ​of Western Sahara’s urban centers and its coastline. It built a security wall in ​the 1980s stretching 2,700 kilometers (about 1,700 miles), leaving most of the territory under its control. The Polisario operates ‌east of ⁠the wall with rear bases in the area of Tindouf in southwestern Algeria, where it administers refugee camps. In 2020, the Polisario said it resumed its “armed struggle” when Morocco took a border crossing with Mauritania. But the UN describes the conflict as “of low intensity.” The UN ​mission has proven unable ​to ensure compliance ⁠with the ceasefire and its initial functions have become outdated, the palace said in the statement. The king urged vigilance in ensuring “strict respect for ​the Kingdom’s territorial integrity, national security and the tranquility of its ​citizens,” it ⁠said. The palace said last week that the end of the UN mission means the withdrawal of the Western Sahara issue from consideration by the Security Council. In an interview with state media ⁠on ​Saturday, Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita said the next step ​for Rabat would be to remove Western Sahara from the UN’s decolonisation committee, saying Rabat had the support of ​two-thirds of UN member states.

items.title: UN panel hails Pakistan’s marriage-age law, flags bonded labour
items.description: • Experts seek details on child brides, rehabilitation of flood victims and reconstruction efforts • Pakistani delegation says 600,000 destroyed homes rebuilt ISLAMABAD: The United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights on Wednesday concluded its review of Pakistan’s second periodic report under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, welcoming the country’s 2025 legal amendment raising the minimum age of marriage to 18. However, committee members raised questions about bonded labour and reconstruction efforts following the 2022 and 2025 floods, among other topics. Committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, Michael Windfuhr, welcomed the 2025 amendment to the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929, which raised the minimum age of marriage to 18 for both males and females. However, he noted that the committee remained concerned about the high number of child brides and asked about the impact of measures taken to prevent child marriage. Lazhari Bouzid, another committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, said bonded labour continued to be prevalent in agriculture and was also found in the informal sector, particularly brick making. Construction companies and government agencies were reportedly complicit in the practice by purchasing bricks produced through debt bondage. He asked how Pakistan had responded to these reports. Mr Windfuhr also asked how the country had coped with the impact of the devastating floods in 2022 and 2025. He inquired whether Pakistan could rebuild housing for affected people and restore their access to land or resources, and how many people remained displaced. ‘Range of measures’ Minister of State for Law and Justice and head of the delegation, Barrister Aqeel Malik, said in his opening remarks that Pakistan had taken a range of legislative, policy and institutional measures since 2017 for the progressive realisation of covenant rights. He said child marriage restraint laws had set the minimum age of marriage at 18 for both boys and girls in Islamabad , Balochistan, Punjab and Sindh, and criminalised child, early and forced marriages. During the ensuing dialogue, the delegation said Pakistan’s Constitution prohibited slavery and all forms of forced labour, while the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1992 had abolished the practice. Punjab had documented more than 210,000 kiln workers, and district vigilance committees had been established in many districts. Labour inspectors had identified more than 2,900 victims of forced labour last year. On flood recovery, the delegation said the government had established a national emergency operations centre focusing on high-risk areas and launched a national flood protection programme. The programme aimed to protect at-risk people, eight million acres of agricultural land and 2.2 million housing units. Each province was also implementing flood protection measures. Of the 2.1 million homes destroyed in the 2022 floods, 600,000 had been rebuilt, while reconstruction of the remaining houses was under way. In her concluding remarks, committee expert and task force leader for Pakistan, Julieta Rossi, said the delegation had outlined processes for implementing economic, social and cultural rights, as well as the significant challenges facing the country and gaps between legislative progress and implementation. “This information would be reflected in the committee’s concluding observations, which the panel hoped that Pakistan would implement in good faith,” she added. Mr Malik said in his concluding remarks that the delegation had outlined its efforts to bridge the gaps between constitutional guarantees and their realisation. “The country’s trajectory was toward the progressive realisation of covenant rights,” he said, adding that despite constraints and challenges, Pakistan had made considerable progress since its first review. “[Pakistan] hopes that the committee’s candour and rigour will help pave the way for the full realisation of economic, social and cultural rights for all,” he added. Committee vice chair and acting chair of the dialogue, Asraf Ally Caunhye, thanked the delegation for its participation in the constructive dialogue and its expression of unwavering commitment to protecting the rights enshrined in the covenant. The Pakistani delegation comprised representatives from the Ministry of Law and Justice, the Ministry of Human Rights and the Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the United Nations Office at Geneva. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: Agalga rejects claims Mahama has shifted position on LGBTQ bill
items.description: Majority Leader James Agalga has rejected claims that President John Mahama has changed his position on the LGBTQ bill. He says errors in the legislation have held up its transmission to the Presidency. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, Mr Agalga said Parliament must correct the bill’s penal provisions before submitting it for assent. “Contrary to all the wild speculations that the president has shifted goalposts and all that. No, he hasn’t.” He placed responsibility for the outstanding work squarely on Parliament. “We have the duty of enacting laws,” he said. Mr Agalga explained that the House discovered inconsistencies after the bill had passed its third reading. These included errors in computing penalty units and provisions that did not align with existing legislation. “For instance, how to compute penalty units was completely done in error, in some cases,” he said. He warned that leaving those defects unresolved would create problems when courts apply the legislation. “Otherwise, the bill as it stands in this current form would have serious challenges when it comes to implementation,” he said. Parliament would therefore have to rescind its third-reading decision. That would allow a second consideration to correct the penalties before the bill returns for passage. “So, not much of substance would change,” Mr Agalga said. The explanation follows months of controversy over the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, 2025, passed on May 29, 2026. The Minority opposed amendments covering professional services, arguing that they weakened the legislation. The Majority maintained that the exemptions clarified existing constitutional protections. The fallout also drew in Speaker Alban Bagbin. He summoned parliamentary leaders after saying the passage had caught him off guard. He called for consensus on the process and implementation. On Tuesday, the Speaker renewed his commitment to completing the bill during the current meeting. He also threatened to publicly identify anyone who obstructed the process. Mr Agalga confirmed that the Speaker would handle the corrections during this meeting. When asked whether the bill would reach the President this month, he replied, “Absolutely.” He maintained that Parliament was the proper forum to resolve the defects and clear the way for transmission to the President.

items.description: Le démocrate Abdul el-Sayed a remporté l'élection sénatoriale dans l'État du Michigan (nord), devenant le premier musulman à être élu au Sénat américain, selon les projections des médias US. Médecin d’origine égyptienne, el-Sayed a battu son adversaire républicain Mike Rogers à l'issue de l'un des duels les plus suivis et les plus coûteux des élections législatives de mi-mandat tenues mardi aux États-Unis. Selon les résultats disponibles mercredi matin, le candidat démocrate a recueilli environ 52 % des suffrages, contre un peu plus de 47 % pour son rival républicain. Ce résultat offre aux démocrates une victoire décisive et leur permet de conserver le siège du Michigan occupé par le sénateur Gary Peters, qui prend sa retraite. « Michigan, nous l'avons fait ! » , a lancé Abdul El-Sayed devant ses partisans réunis à Detroit, dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi, à l'annonce de sa victoire. Omniprésent sur les réseaux sociaux, Abdul El-Sayed a attiré les foules lors de ses meetings électoraux à travers le Michigan, y compris dans des bastions républicains profondément conservateurs. Au cœur de son programme électoral figurait notamment la réforme du système de santé américain, dont il a dénoncé le coût élevé et la forte dépendance à l'égard du secteur privé. « Vous devriez pouvoir consulter un médecin sans recevoir une facture exorbitante », déclarait il à la veille du scrutin, plaidant pour un accès plus abordable aux soins. Il a également fait de la lutte contre l'influence de l'argent en politique l'un de ses chevaux de bataille, se présentant comme le candidat du changement face à des responsables politiques jugés trop liés aux intérêts économiques. Outre son entrée historique en tant que premier sénateur musulman, Abdul El-Sayed devrait également devenir le premier médecin démocrate à siéger au Sénat depuis 1969. The post Midterms : le démocrate Abdul el-Sayed devient le premier musulman élu au Sénat US appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: ‘Absolutely’ – Agalga confirms LGBTQ bill will reach Mahama this month
items.description: Majority Leader James Agalga says the LGBTQ bill will reach President John Dramani Mahama this month, after Parliament corrects errors in its penalty provisions. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, Agalga gave an emphatic response when asked whether the bill would go before the President this month. “Absolutely,” he said. Asked whether that would happen before Parliament rises, he added: “Yes, yes, yes.” The assurance sets a new deadline for legislation that has sparked fierce political exchanges, legal challenges, and criticism from human rights advocates. An earlier version passed in February 2024 drew international condemnation and warnings about its impact on Ghana’s development funding. It never became law. Then-President Nana Akufo-Addo withheld assent pending legal challenges, and the bill subsequently lapsed. Parliament passed a revived version in May 2026. However, concerns over its punishment provisions forced another review. The House went on recess in July without completing that process. Mr Agalga said the latest delay stemmed from errors Parliament itself needed to correct. “For instance, how to compute penalty units was completely done in error, in some cases,” he said. He explained that the penalties did not properly align with existing legislation. Leaving them unchanged would create difficulties when courts imposed sentences. “Otherwise, the bill as it stands in this current form would have serious challenges when it comes to implementation,” he warned. The correction requires Parliament to rescind its decision at the third-reading stage. That would allow a second consideration to address the defective provisions. “So, not much of substance would change,” Mr Agalga said. His explanation comes amid renewed pressure to complete work on the bill. On Tuesday, Speaker Alban Bagbin warned that he would publicly identify anyone who obstructed the process. Asked about presidential assent, Agalga rejected suggestions that Mahama had changed his position. “It’s Parliament’s work. We have the duty of enacting laws,” he said. He maintained that lawmakers must first resolve the problems they had identified. “We think that we are the proper forum to correct those anomalies to pave the way for the bill to be transmitted to the president.”
