items.title: TraffiTech-GH: Mahama directs installation of speed camera warning signs for transparency
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has directed the authorities implementing the TraffiTech-GH traffic enforcement system to install clear warning signs ahead of speed camera locations to alert motorists and promote transparency. He said motorists must be given advance notice of camera locations as part of efforts to build public confidence in the new road safety initiative. The President said although the technology was intended to curb dangerous driving, its implementation must be accompanied by measures that inform motorists about its operation. Speaking on the sidelines of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) at Jumby Bay Island in Antigua and Barbuda, President Mahama stressed that transparency was essential when introducing technology-driven traffic enforcement. “All I will urge is that the police and those implementing Traffitech should put signs showing where the cameras are, because that is one of the things you need to do if you are introducing this kind of innovation. You need to put signposts warning motorists that there is a speed camera ahead. I think that transparency is important,” he said. Road safety cannot wait President Mahama also pushed back against arguments that the government should first repair the country’s roads and improve related infrastructure before deploying the traffic monitoring system. He said the poor condition of some roads should not be used as a reason to postpone measures aimed at reducing speeding and preventing road crashes. To underline the urgency, he drew attention to the number of schoolchildren who are knocked down by vehicles, particularly while returning home from school, with some suffering fatal injuries or permanent disabilities. “If you look at the number of children knocked down every year in Ghana when they are coming from school, you will understand why it is important for us to check over speeding. Children coming from school are knocked down and killed or permanently injured, and so it is important for us to check speeding,” he told The 1957 News. The president maintained that traffic enforcement and road infrastructure improvements should proceed alongside each other rather than be treated as competing priorities. He cited the United Kingdom as an example, arguing that speed cameras were used there despite roads not being in perfect condition. “My understanding is that Traffitech has begun with overspeeding; they have not yet added the other components of jumping red lights and parking wrongly,” he said. Responding to calls for road repairs to precede the introduction of the system, he added: “I mean, it doesn’t happen like that. The roads are not perfect in the UK, and yet they have speed cameras.” More enforcement measures expected President Mahama indicated that the current phase of TraffiTech-GH was primarily focused on detecting and penalising motorists who exceed prescribed speed limits. Other traffic violations, including running red lights and illegal parking, are expected to form part of the broader enforcement framework. The system is intended to strengthen traffic law enforcement through technology and address dangerous driving practices that contribute to road crashes. The President’s comments suggest that public education and clear notification of camera locations should accompany any expansion of the system. ‘Don’t overspeed’ On concerns that the fines imposed under TraffiTech-GH were too expensive, President Mahama said motorists could avoid the penalties by complying with speed limits. He was emphatic that drivers who stayed within the legally prescribed limits had no reason to incur speeding fines. “If it is too expensive, then don’t overspeed, that’s all, there is a solution to it,” he said. His comments come amid public debate over the introduction of automated traffic enforcement, particularly the cost of penalties and whether the country’s road infrastructure is adequate to support stricter enforcement. The President, however, maintained that preventing avoidable deaths and injuries should remain a priority, while insisting that the implementation of the technology must be transparent and accompanied by adequate public information.

items.title: Parliament to reverse LGBTQ bill’s passage over errors in penalties – Agalga
items.description: Parliament will rescind the passage of the anti-LGBTQ bill to correct errors in its penalty provisions, Majority Leader James Agalga has disclosed. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he said mistakes in calculating penalty units could create serious problems when courts apply the proposed law. “For instance, how to compute penalty units was completely done in error, in some cases,” he said. The House will therefore reverse its approval at the third-reading stage. That will allow lawmakers to reopen consideration of the bill and correct the provisions before sending it to the President. “The penal provisions are not aligned. They are not aligned properly,” Mr Agalga said. He explained that the penalties must align with existing legislation. The corrections would leave the bill’s substance largely intact. “So, not much of substance would change.” The planned reversal follows months of controversy over the bill’s May 29 passage. Speaker Alban Bagbin subsequently directed Parliament to revisit the process. He raised concerns about procedural compliance and whether the bipartisan support recorded at committee level was reflected on the floor. Then Majority Leader Mahama Ayariga defended the passage and maintained that Parliament had followed its rules. The legislation also triggered disagreements over proposed exemptions for journalists, lawyers and health professionals. Critics within Parliament argued that the changes weakened the bill. Its defenders maintained that the exemptions protected legitimate professional duties. Mr Agalga said the latest intervention concerned how the penalties would be applied in practice. “Otherwise, the bill as it stands in this current form would have serious challenges when it comes to implementation,” he warned. He confirmed that Parliament intended to complete the corrections during the current meeting. Asked whether the bill would reach the President this month, he replied: “Absolutely”. He also rejected suggestions that the delay reflected a change in the President’s position. “Contrary to all the wild speculations that the President has shifted goalposts and all that. No, he hasn’t.” Mr Agalga said Parliament had identified the defects and was responsible for fixing them before transmission. “We have the duty of enacting laws,” he said.

items.title: Analysis: Midterms clip Trump’s wings at home, not abroad
items.description: THE world had good reason to watch the US midterm elections with bated breath, because their outcome would not only determine the balance of power in Washington, but also shape the course of major international conflicts — particularly in the Middle East — and establish how much political bandwidth Presi­dent Donald Trump would retain to pursue his foreign policy during the final two years of his presidency. The verdict has been considerably harsher than many had anticipated, chiefly beca­use of the fallout of the Iran war. As the election outcome was influenced by an external issue, the implications will ac­c­ordingly be reflected more on the foreign policy front. For foreign capitals, the significance of the result lies less in the change of congressional control itself but what it means for Trump’s ability, and willingness, to use American power abroad. A midterm defeat does not automatically diminish presidential authority over foreign affairs and military operations. Trump, therefore, retains considerable discretion over military operations and negotiations, as well as executive powers over sanctions and trade. What he has actually lost is political room to manoeuvre as Democrats in the Congress can now investigate, obstruct funding and impose greater scrutiny on his decisions. Compounding that would be the fact that some key Republicans, mindful of their own electoral prospects in 2028, may become less willing to defend his policies that come with a political cost. The resulting situation could constrain the president over time, but it would not necessarily make him more cautious in the immediate term. Iran Iran will be the immediate test of how Trump responds to the Republican rout. The electoral setback has created a paradox for the president because while the war is the key reason for the debacle, many think he may still be tempted to intensify military pressure in the hope of securing a decisive outcome before the political space for doing so narrows further. Christopher Clary, a non-resident fellow at Stimson Center, points out that “the Constitution grants the president enormous latitude on the use of force and the president can escalate despite the new Democratic Congress.” But escalation carries the risk of aggravating the original problem. Iranian retaliation in that case could deepen the economic pressures and make the war an even greater political liability. The indications from Tehran further suggest that resumption of full-scale hostilities could also lead to widening of the conflict. Importantly, Trump has a crucial window of two months before the new Congress takes office. But after the transition, political calculations will change with Democrats making the Iran war a major focus of oversight. They could also pursue War Powers resolutions, requiring congressional authorisation for continued hostilities, in addition to attaching conditions or restrictions to defence appropriations. Mr Clary warned that “the lame duck period before the new Congress is sworn in will be an especially dangerous time.” He emphasised that while there are “no real binding constraints on Trump”, the Democrats can “use their budgetary authority to deny new funds to sustain the operation”. The control of spending will give Democrats additional leverage, although it will not automatically enable them to terminate military operations because Trump retains veto power, which he has hinted that he will use, and Democrats don’t command the two-thirds majority needed to override it. Moreover, Democrats will not either want to be seen as curtailing support for American forces. Quincy Institute Vice President Trita Parsi recalled that “the Vietnam war ended because Congress stopped funding it”, adding, “Democrats can do this to Trump’s illegal Iran war as well. If they don’t, they will become complicit”. Sustaining an open ended campaign will, in any case, become politically more difficult and even Republicans, conscious of the electoral cost of the Iran war, may also become increasingly reluctant to support additional funding without a clearer strategy and exit plan. If things do come to that point sometime next year, Trump can then become inclined towards a combination of military pressure and diplomacy by extracting concessions from Tehran through the threat of further strikes while pursuing an agreement, which he can present as an achievement and a resolution of the conflict. Pakistan For Pakistan, the Democrat victory presents a more gradual test. The turnaround in relations under Trump depended heavily on the president and his inner circle, rather than an actual shift in the relationship. Islamabad had moved quickly to cultivate ties with the new administration after Trump returned to office — extraditing the accused in Abbey Gate Kabul bombing; praising the president’s intervention in the May 2025 conflict with India; nominating him for the Nobel Peace prize; and, joining his Board of Peace for Gaza. The unprecedented White House working lunch with Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir in June 2025 — sans PM Shehbaz Sharif — further underscored the importance of the military channel. Critical minerals and cryptocurrency also became prominent areas of engagement, alongside proposals involving Trump family-backed World Liberty Financial, the Roosevelt Hotel and drone manufacturing. A Democratic Congress is unlikely to undo the relationship, but it could subject some of these dealings to greater scrutiny. Questions may be raised about foreign links of the Trump family’s commercial interests, the cooperation with Powerus and Pakistan’s governance and transparency. Mentioning these aspects, Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council noted that “scrutiny of Trump and his family’s business dealings will increase… If so, that could spell bad news for Pakistan.” Erik Sperling, executive director of Just Foreign Policy, recalled earlier congressional letters and legislation initiated by Democrats, raising concerns about the situation in Pakistan, and expected that with Democrats now controlling the House, these measures will have a clear path to floor votes. Islamabad’s earlier effort to secure a $10bn US Treasury financial backstop has found little enthusiasm, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent emphasising self-reliance and IMF reforms. A Democratic controlled Congress would make congressional support for a large financial arrangement even more difficult. There will, nevertheless, be areas of bipartisan convergence, particularly counterterrorism, regional stability, critical minerals and Pakistan’s diplomatic role in the Iran conflict. The challenge for Islamabad will be to translate the access secured under Trump into a relationship with a wider institutional base, including engagement with Democrats and a stronger case for durable economic cooperation. Other arenas A Democratic Congress could help preserve military and economic support for Ukraine and scrutinise arms transfers to Israel, without forcing Trump to abandon his preference for a negotiated settlement with Moscow or bringing about an abrupt change in US policy towards Israel. Adam Weinstein, deputy Middle East director at the Quincy Institute, said: “Uncritical support for Israel, and more importantly, close ties to AIPAC, have become serious political liabilities in the US. These results reflect that shift.” Noted commentator Max Blumenthal said that while “the ‘special relationship’ with Israel was once a matter of bipartisan unity among party elites, it’s become a polarising wedge issue and a poison pill for any president”. He pointed out that Trump, while realising the gravity of the situation, had announced that he will cut $4 billion in annual aid to Israel, in a last-ditch bid to salvage the Republican situation ahead of the polls. Saudi Arabia, too, may face closer scrutiny over nuclear cooperation and security commitments, while the UAE and Egypt could encounter greater congressional attention to human rights and military assistance. On China, strategic competition is likely to remain bipartisan, although Democrats may place greater emphasis on alliances and supply chain resilience. They may also seek to reclaim some congressional oversight over tariffs and trade. Washington-based analyst Shuja Nawaz thinks “Cuba may be the easiest target for President Trump. He might also try his hand at summitry with Putin and Xi but it is unlikely to gain much. They have consistently outplayed him”. After facing increased opposition to his domestic agenda, Trump may now turn increasingly to foreign policy, trade and military decisions, where his executive authority is wider, but international partners will have to consider whether commitments made by this administration can survive a change of political direction in Washington, come 2028. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: Riyadh rolls over $3bn as prospects of $10bn US facility wane
items.description: • Aurangzeb says proposed US facility is not essential, would provide additional support if secured • Further Eurobond, Panda bond and rupee-linked dollar-settled issuances planned • Govt targets $4bn reduction in external debt ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has secured a $3 billion rollover from Saudi Arabia, as prospects of a proposed $10bn US backstop facility appear to have waned, it emerged on Wednesday. Speaking to journalists at Parliament House, Finance Minister Muhammad Auran­gzeb confirmed that Riyadh had extended the $3bn financing it provided in April this year to bridge a gap arising from $3.5bn in repayments to the United Arab Emirates. “It has been extended and for a reasonable period. You don’t need to worry as to for how long given the kind of strategic relationship we have,” he said when asked about the facility, which matured on Oct 31 under its three-month term. He said he had a very good meeting with his Saudi counterpart, Mohammed Al-Jadaan, during the recent World Bank-IMF meetings in Bangkok. Saudi Arabia had already extended its $5bn facility until 2028. Asked whether Pakistan had also sought additional support, the minister categorically denied it, saying this was not needed as foreign exchange reserves covered more than three months of imports and would be strengthened to provide a four-month import cover by the end of the year through capital markets. Responding to another question about the prospects of the $10bn Exchange Stabilisation Support Facility (ESSF) requested from the US in July this year, he sought to lower expectations that he himself had raised over the past several months. “What we asked for back in July and were looking at was the market access. We have got the market access,” he said, referring to the $3bn bond Pakistan issued in September against orders worth $6bn. “If that (ESSF) materialises, fantastic, it will be a liquidity support facility. Otherwise, we have plans for further Eurobond issuance, Panda bond issuance and rupee-linked dollar-settled bond,” the minister said. He added that he had held meetings with 70-80 institutional investors in Bangkok, who had a very clear view of Pakistan, and that offers were available for five-year and 10-year maturities, “because clearly we are looking beyond the [IMF] programme”. He said the government was looking at the US from a broader perspective, as the US Export-Import Bank and Development Finance Corporation (DFC) needed to support their investors and exporters in Pakistan. “That is real financing and real credit,” he said, adding that the ESSF request was for a liquidity support facility to help the sovereign. “If possible, fine; if not, we are going to move forward, with or without it.” The finance minister also reported that the IMF Executive Board meeting to approve a disbursement of $1.2bn to Pakistan would be held in December. External debt Earlier, he told the Senate Standing Committee on Finance that Pakistan was targeting a reduction of $4bn in external debt during the current fiscal year and $3.5bn next year, compared with $4.5bn in the last fiscal year. He said the government was seeking to replace expensive short-term borrowing with longer-maturity financing through bonds and private placements to reduce refinancing risks. He said external debt had been rising by $5-6bn annually, from $45bn in 2014-15 to around $100bn, but had increased by only $1bn annually over the past two years. “Our objective is not to increase external debt. All the transactions like Eurobond, Panda bond or private placements have been replacement bonds to replace expensive with cheaper facilities,” he said, adding that fiscal discipline had helped contain the fiscal and current account deficits and, despite oil and wheat import bills, the current account deficit would be no more than 1pc this year. “This is hard-earned stability that helped create buffers to meet our requirements despite floods and war in the region, and foreign exchange reserves crossed $21.5bn, which is the best-ever level of reserves in our history,” he said, adding that Pakistan could not afford to lose this basic hygiene. Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told the committee, which was presided over by Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, that public debt had declined to 68.6pc of GDP by the end of June 2026, from 75.1pc in fiscal year 2022-23. Year-on-year growth in public debt had slowed to 7.7pc in the last fiscal year, the lowest in 20 years, he said. The secretary said domestic debt amounted to Rs58.8 trillion by the end of August 2026, down from Rs68.4tr at the end of June, while foreign debt remained stable at $98.2bn. He reported net financing requirements of $11bn after rollovers and refinancing, of which $5bn had already been repaid in the first four months of the current fiscal year. The remaining $6bn was payable over the next seven months. The committee took strong exception to the difficulties faced by parliamentarians in obtaining foreign exchange for personal travel, saying the humiliation they faced at the hands of banks and the central bank was unacceptable. Mr Mandviwalla directed the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to review existing procedures, including clearance requirements relating to politically exposed persons (PEPs) and the mandatory personal appearance of parliamentarians before exchange companies, despite their submission of valid passports, tickets and visas. The committee also expressed serious displeasure over the SBP’s response, dated Oct 30, 2026, to a letter sent by the committee secretary on its behalf to the SBP governor. It observed that the matter had been addressed by a deputy director-level officer instead of an appropriately senior authority. The chairman termed the requirement for personal appearance humiliating and called for an immediate review of the existing procedures, warning that the committee would take serious notice if the matter remained unresolved. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: Taunsa farmers hit hard by closure of Chashma Canal
items.description: — Dawn LAHORE/DERA GHAZI KHAN: The closure of Chashma Right Bank Canal (CRBC), especially in its stretch falling in Punjab, has been affecting farmers badly due to inadequate repair/maintenance and water theft as there seems to be none in the provincial and federal governments to listen to the affected. The situation worsened after a portion of the CRBC — an inter-provincial canal irrigating huge chunks of land in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab – was breached, forcing the Water and Power Development Authority to stop releasing water into the canal from the Chashma Barrage over Indus. “You cannot imagine the situation we have been in for a long time. In Kharif (April), we received 77pc water shortage, followed by May, June, July and August wherein we witnessed 78pc, 95pc, 98pc and 96pc shortage, respectively, in our command area,” reveals an officer of the Punjab Irrigation Department. The situation, according to him, worsened further when the canal was breached in Paharpur tehsil of KP in September, leaving authorities with no option but to stop releasing water to CRBC. “Since September, we have no water and the canal banks have not been repaired. It seems no one is taking this matter on a priority basis,” the official deplored. The CRBC is an inter-provincial gravity irrigation system serving KP and Punjab. During Kharif 2026, Punjab suffered a severe canal water shortage despite substantial flows at the Chashma. The CRBC command area consists of approximately 606,000 acres, of which 240,000 acres (about 97,125 hectares) are in Punjab. The main canal is about 274km long, including a 103km reach in Punjab, which receives its supply at RD-513. The system/head design discharge is about 4,825 cusecs and the Punjab’s design capacity is 1,834 cusecs, with an operational daily indent of 1,800 cusecs, served by 30 distributaries and 32 minors totalling about 440km. Groundwater in much of the Punjab command is brackish and unsuitable for irrigation. “The closure has disrupted planned irrigation regime in the Punjab command area. The cumulative deficit during the Kharif season, coupled with zero supplies during the latter part of September, has exposed crops to severe water stress and increased the risk of production losses,” he added. Wapda had constructed CRBC during 1998-2002 as a perennial canal off-taking from the right bank of Chashma Barrage (design discharge 4,825 cusecs), including the canal system, outlets and chakbandi. In May 2002, distributaries and minors D-24 to D-53 in Punjab were handed over to the Punjab Irrigation Department under a formal agreement, while the main canal and its structures, including 21 cross-drainage structures, remained with Wapda. Following a Council of Common Interests (CCI) decision of Aug 8, 2020, and a bilateral agreement on March 14, 2022, the Punjab section of the main canal and its structures was handed over to the Punjab Irrigation Department/CRBC Division, Taunsa Sharif. The operational control of upper portion of the main canal still remains under the Wapda authorities. The official correspondence reveals that the irrigation authorities repeatedly raised the issue of inadequate supplies with Wapda. “The situation further deteriorated when a major breach in the main canal at RD 185 Left, within the KP portion, took place on Sept 14, 2026. Head supplies remained suspended on Sept 15 and 16, and the discharge at the Punjab border (RD 513) remained zero from Sept 17 to 30,” the official said. He said according to information, Wapda authorities awarded the emergency works for closure of the breach and concrete lining of critical reaches on Sept 30, 2026, at a total bid cost of approximately Rs385 million. The rehabilitation work is presently under execution at site, with an estimated completion period of about 45 days. “Until completion of the works and restoration of canal operation, Punjab area remains deprived of its normal canal supplies,” he added. According to him, the actual extent of crop damage and financial loss should be prepared through a properly documented field assessment, including crop-wise and area-wise verification, in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Cost Sharing Agreement. He said the shortage of water supplies to Punjab during the Kharif season was due to illegal extraction and theft of water from the canal by the farmers in KP. “We have been told by the KP irrigation authorities that as many as 1,000 cusecs of water is allegedly stolen by the people in KP,” he said. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: US federal court blocks Afghan deportation plan
items.description: WASHINGTON: A US federal court blocked on Tuesday the Trump administration’s plans to deport scores of Afghan immigrants back to Afghanistan, a move advocacy groups said could endanger their lives. Judge Valerie Caproni of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled that the United States could not send any Afghan nationals to Afghanistan or Pakistan this week. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Deputy Assistant Director Christopher George told the court there were “no planned or confirmed chartered or commercial flights” to deport Afghan nationals in the US to Afghanistan or Pakistan this week, according to court documents. US media reported last week that more than 150 Afghans in the US would be deported via Pakistan to Afghanistan as part of President Donald Trump’s latest immigration crackdown. Among the group were relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies. “A week ago, there was a plane. Today, the government told a federal judge there isn’t one,” AfghanEvac President Shawn VanDiver said in a statement after Tuesday’s ruling. “That didn’t happen by accident. Veterans, advocates, 66 members of Congress, and thousands of Americans got this flight stopped,” he added. Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities voiced “serious concern” on Monday over the reported deportation plans. Advocacy groups have warned that the removal of former allies and their families could endanger their lives. After regaining power in 2021, Taliban authorities announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and governments and have repeated promises this year that their former foes could safely return home. But the United Nations has recorded reports of extrajudicial killings, detentions and abuses. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: Exports to Europe dip despite GSP+
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Despite having Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP+) status, Pakistan’s exports to major western and eastern European markets fell in the first quarter of 2026-27 compared with the previous year. Overall exports to Europe dipped modestly, with a slight increase in proceeds from southern and northern European countries during the July-September quarter, raising serious concerns for policymakers. The ongoing Middle East conflict has accelerated the decline in exports to these markets, along with the European Union’s preferential market access offered to India, one of Pakistan’s key competitors in textiles. Data compiled by the State Bank of Pakistan showed that exports to European countries contracted 1.84pc to $2.350 billion in 1QFY27 from $2.394bn a year ago. Trade analysts warn that the Middle East conflict could further dampen export demand, as rising energy costs are likely to squeeze consumer spending in Europe, which is already under strain from the economic fallout of the Ukraine war. Exports to northern Europe increased by 21.07pc to $236.321m in 1QFY27 from $195.191m a year ago. Exports to southern Europe grew 5.26pc to $879.896m in 1QFY27 from $835.862m in the corresponding period last year. In this region, exports to Spain rose 17.78pc to $451.244m from $383.122m in the preceding year. Exports to Italy declined 8.49pc to $298.731m in 1QFY27, compared with $326.460m in the same period last year. Exports to Greece grew 3.52pc to $34.961m during the months under review, compared with $33.774m over the previous year. However, exports to eastern Europe fell 15.05pc to $168.761m in 1QFY27 from $198.677m. Before Brexit, the United Kingdom was Pakistan’s major export destination. In the post-Brexit period, Pakistan’s exports to the UK increased 6.64pc to $612.305m in 1QFY27 from $574.171m a year ago. Western Europe, which includes countries such as Germany, the Netherlands, France, Italy, and Belgium, accounts for the largest share of Pakistan’s exports to the EU. However, exports to this region shrank 8.51pc to $1.065bn in 1QFY27 from $1.164bn in 1QFY26. Exports to Germany dipped 12.77pc to $389.116m in 1QFY27 from $446.100m. Similarly, exports to the Netherlands, the second-largest market for Pakistani goods, fell by 3.07pc to $370.005m from $381.752m a year ago. Exports to France fell by 0.47pc to $136.030m in 1QFY27 from $136.686m, followed by a 7.57pc decline to Belgium’s $127.431m against $137.871m. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: Foreign ministry told to tighten accounting rules
items.description: ISLAMABAD: A parliamentary committee on Wednesday criticised the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for having no control over funds management and lax accounting procedures, instructing its new secretary Asim Iftikhar Ahmad to streamline and tighten accounting procedures and make rules and share them with the committee. The directive came after the Public Accounts Committee, while discussing audit objections of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs 2024-25, observed that its staff posted in foreign missions was embezzling and mismanaging public funds without accountability. One case in particular caused massive losses to the public exchequer, when an ex-accountant posted in the Pakistan embassy in Vienna, Austria, fraudulently drew 442,256 euros and $134,292 over a period of two years. Officials from the office of Auditor General of Pakistan suspected that the former accountant was not alone in tampering and transferring the public money into his personal and wife’s bank accounts and that senior officials in the Pakistani Mission were also involved in the scam. PAC told staff posted in foreign missions ‘embezzling funds’ The PAC expressed strong dissatisfaction with Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) for failing to recover the embezzled amount after a case was registered against the ex-accountant, Muhammad Sulaiman Qureshi, six years ago. Members of the panel were more surprised upon learning that Muhammad Sulaiman Qureshi was in Pakistan and he has been out on bail. The chairman of the committee, MNA Naveed Qamar, directed officials concerned to summon the FIA director general for a better response. Similarly, another accountant, during posting in Pakistan emb­assy in Sofia, Bulgaria, also frau­dulently withdrew 56,499 Lev and $74,415 between 2018-23. Audit officials expressed concern that the misappropriated public money had still not been recovered from the accountant. Furthermore, the accountant, after being dismissed from service, approached courts, which reinstated him in service. In response to failure to recover the embezzled amount, the PAC chairman directed that officials investigating fraud should be exempted from travel bans introduced under austerity measures. In another case pertaining to unjustified retention of heavy balance of Higher Education Commission (HEC) on account of overseas scholarship in the US, amounting to $4.5 million, the PAC expressed surprise why the funds had not been disbursed among needy students. “The Pakistani mission did not have clear instructions from HEC on the matter,” said Asim Iftikhar Ahmad. In response, Mr Qamar argued that HEC should be held accountable over this. Similarly, in another matter pertaining to unauthorised borrowing of loan from HEC’s account of 360,000 euros, Mr Ahmad said that his office was in process of returning funds to the commission. In the case of unjustified blockage of government funds in an unauthorised suspense account in Dhaka, Bangladesh, a sum of $1.143m was parked idle. Audit officials observed that holding a huge amount in suspense account without approval of the finance division was a clear violation of rules, which required settlement of inevitable payment at the earliest. They also observed that the Pakistani mission maintaining the US dollar account in the name of suspense account for payment of rent of chancery whose ownership issue was disputed, had not been resolved yet. The PAC referred the matter to departmental accounts committee. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: Swat basin faces over 5°C warming by century’s end
items.description: ISLAMABAD: A glacier risk assessment of the Swat watershed has war­ned that the basin is expected to warm by more than 5°C by the end of the century, particularly bet­ween October and June. Winter rainfall is expected to change little, but summer rainfall could more than double under some climate scenarios, according to the assessment carried out by the Green Climate Fund (GCF), with support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB). The changes are likely to increase the risk of severe floods and erosion, cause a short-term rise in water availability due to glacier melt and runoff, and lead to long-term declines as glaciers continue to recede, according to the assessment made available on Wednesday. The Swat basin, which has more than 10,000 glaciers, faces an increased risk of infrastructure failure and resulting floods. The assessment also warned of agricultural losses, erosion in valley areas, and a short-term water surplus followed by a long-term deficit. The GCF has conducted glacier risk assessments for four representative wat­e­rsheds: Kura (Arme­nia, Azerbaijan and Georgia), Naryn (Kyrgyz Republic, with downstream links to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan), Pyanj (Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Afghanistan) and Swat (Hindu Kush-Karakoram-Himalaya). The four pilot basins capture diverse glacier and hydrological conditions across Central and West Asia. Together, they illustrate how elevation, glacier mass and snow duration shape regional water supplies and risks. These assessments serve as initial pilots under the ‘Glacier to Farms’ (G2F) programme and complement the existing ADB country-level climate risk assessments. Although only four basins were studied, they were strategically selected to represent the nine developing member countries covered by G2F and inform the programme’s future expansion to other transboundary watersheds and basins in the region. The climate risk and capacity assessment of the four glacier-fed watersheds in Central and West Asia highlights accelerating glacier retreat, growing water security risks and priority actions to strengthen resilience, adaptation and regional cooperation. The assessment analysed 40 years of weather records to identify spatial and temporal variations in temperature, rainfall and snowfall across mountain and lowland areas. Historical data were used to bias-correct global climate models to improve their local accuracy. Statistical clustering of multiple models produced basin-specific projections focused on glacier, snow and permafrost areas, providing a realistic basis for understanding future climate impacts across the G2F region. It analysed long-term temperature, precipitation and cryosphere trends across the four watersheds to establish a regional baseline and develop future scenarios for 2035, 2055, 2085 and 2100. Using multi-model climate datasets validated against regional observations, the analysis identified key impact pathways, sectoral risks and opportunities to strengthen resilience in agriculture, energy and human settlements. Across the G2F basins, temperatures are projected to rise by around 3°C to 5°C by the end of the century, accelerating the loss of glaciers, snow and permafrost. Seasonal water availability will shift, with earlier snowmelt and river flow peaks, while hotter summers will increase drought risks and water demand. Although some areas may receive more winter precipitation, overall water availability will decline as glacier-fed runoff diminishes. The assessment examines how projected changes in temperature, precipitation and glacier mass will affect hazards, water resources and livelihoods across the G2F region. It highlights the main risks — glacier retreat, slope instability and shifting water availability — and explains how these processes interact to shape local and downstream impacts. Risks associated with glacier melt and extreme events, such as glacial lake outburst floods (Glofs) and landslides, are already high across High Mountain Asia and are expected to intensify as the climate continues to warm. However, the assessment notes that appropriate resilience measures can reduce these risks to manageable levels. As glaciers and permafrost melt, slopes and natural dams become unstable, increasing the likelihood of rockfalls, ice avalanches and Glofs. Such events can travel long distances, threatening homes, roads and other infrastructure in mountainous and downstream areas. Heavier rain and snowfall, followed by rapid spring melting, are likely to trigger flash floods and debris flows. Inadequate watershed management will exacerbate these effects, accelerating soil erosion, degrading water quality and compromising the integrity of dams and irrigation systems. Higher temperatures will increase water demand, particularly during summer. Glacier melt has historically provided a buffer against drought in the region, but this buffer will disappear as glaciers retreat and heatwaves intensify, reducing water supplies when they are most needed. Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

items.title: Bensaid annonce près de 800 terrains de proximité et la révision de la loi sur les fédérations sportives
items.description: Le ministre de la Jeunesse, de la Culture et de la Communication, Mohamed Mehdi Bensaid, a annoncé la mise en service de près de 800 terrains de proximité au cours de l’année en cours, avec une attention particulière accordée aux communes rurales et aux périphéries urbaines, dans un contexte de demande croissante en infrastructures sportives de la part des collectivités territoriales et des citoyens. Lors de la présentation du projet de budget sectoriel de son département devant la Commission de l’enseignement, de la culture et de la communication à la Chambre des représentants, mercredi, Bensaid a souligné que le ministère accorde une importance particulière à l’élargissement de la pratique sportive et à la garantie d’une répartition territoriale équitable des infrastructures. Il a insisté sur le droit des citoyens au sport, la nécessité de s’ouvrir aux partenaires et de promouvoir le sport dans les quartiers et les douars, tout en associant les fédérations sportives à l’encadrement des activités à l’échelle locale. Concernant la gestion du secteur, le responsable gouvernemental a affirmé que le ministère entend accompagner les fédérations sportives confrontées à des dysfonctionnements organisationnels et contribuer à leur résolution. Une commission a ainsi été constituée afin d’accorder aux fédérations concernées des délais pour régulariser leur situation, avant le recours aux dispositions légales. Cette démarche s’inscrit dans le prolongement de l’expérience d’accompagnement des difficultés rencontrées par la Fédération royale marocaine de basketball lors de la précédente législature. Le ministre a également indiqué que deux commissions provisoires assurent actuellement la gestion de la Fédération royale marocaine de pétanque et de la Fédération royale marocaine de badminton. Il a rappelé le droit du ministère de tutelle d’intervenir en cas de dysfonctionnements dans la gestion des instances sportives, précisant que la même démarche est engagée pour traiter les problèmes que connaissent les fédérations de tennis de table, de natation, de cricket, de hockey, de kick-boxing, de tir et de motocyclisme. Bensaid a par ailleurs fait état de la volonté du ministère de réviser la loi régissant le fonctionnement des fédérations sportives au Maroc, dans le but de renforcer la gouvernance et de remédier à plusieurs dispositions devenues obsolètes. Cette révision sera précédée d’une consultation des fédérations, appelées à présenter leurs propositions et observations sur les amendements envisagés. S’agissant de la lutte contre les actes de hooliganisme et les comportements négatifs dans les stades, le ministre a expliqué que son département adopte une approche préventive, à la fois sécuritaire et organisationnelle. Celle-ci repose notamment sur la modernisation des enceintes sportives et leur équipement en caméras de surveillance et en systèmes de suivi précis, en coordination avec les autorités sécuritaires compétentes. Le responsable gouvernemental a également fait état de progrès dans la lutte contre le marché noir et les dysfonctionnements liés à la vente des billets de matchs. Ces avancées reposent sur la numérisation intégrale du processus de vente à travers des applications électroniques et sur l’abandon progressif des billets papier. Il a, dans ce cadre, souligné la responsabilité directe des clubs sportifs dans l’encadrement de leurs supporters et leur contribution à la gestion sécuritaire des grandes rencontres, ainsi que dans l’organisation et l’accompagnement des déplacements des supporters entre les provinces et les préfectures. Au titre du bilan des activités sportives, Bensaid a indiqué que le Maroc a accueilli près de 100 grandes manifestations sportives durant l’année en cours. Parmi les principaux événements, il a cité la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2025, la Coupe d’Afrique des nations de futsal 2026 et le Championnat d’Afrique de football des moins de 23 ans. Le ministre a qualifié d’importants les résultats sportifs obtenus par le Royaume, évoquant notamment les sacres du Maroc à la CAN 2025 et à la CAN de futsal 2026, ainsi que les performances positives enregistrées lors de la dernière Coupe du monde et les exploits des clubs nationaux dans les compétitions continentales. The post Bensaid annonce près de 800 terrains de proximité et la révision de la loi sur les fédérations sportives appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: European left-wing figures highlight CPC's commitment to self-reform
items.description: European left-wing political figures have highlighted the importance of the Communist Party of China's (CPC) commitment to self-reform, saying its experience in maintaining Party discipline and putting people first offers valuable lessons for left-wing parties in Europe. "People-centric development doesn't happen spontaneously. It needs a strong party that's disciplined," said Kaivon Kjems, international secretary of the Communist Party of Denmark. He noted that self-reform enables a party to identify and address challenges within society, navigate competing interests and remain responsive to people's concerns. Kjems said European left-wing parties could learn from the CPC's experience, stressing that meaningful efforts to address people's concerns require serious commitment to self-reform and strong party building. He added that the CPC's people-oriented approach offers concrete lessons in tackling the problems people face in their daily lives. Adam Barbato Shoufani, general secretary of the Swiss Communist Youth, described the CPC's self-reform process as central to its commitment to serving the people. "The Communist Party of China is serving the people, not the entrepreneurs, not the big capital, financial capital of foreign investors," he said, adding that initiating a process of self-reform demonstrates political courage. The two shared their views with CGTN on Tuesday during the 16th World Socialism Forum in Beijing. The forum, which ran from Tuesday to Wednesday, brought together more than 80 participants from 40 countries, including leaders of foreign communist parties, prominent Marxist scholars, social activists and diplomats from foreign missions in China.

items.title: Transport routier : nouvelle aide de 400 millions de DH
items.description: L’Exécutif débloque une enveloppe d’environ 400 millions de dirhams pour une nouvelle aide exceptionnelle aux professionnels du transport routier, au titre de la période du 1er au 15 novembre. Toutes les catégories de véhicules sont concernées, dans un contexte de fluctuation des prix des carburants. Le ministre du Transport et de la Logistique, Abdessamad Kayouh, a annoncé que l’Exécutif mobilise une enveloppe d’environ 400 millions de dirhams (MDH) pour un nouveau soutien exceptionnel en faveur des professionnels du transport routier. Cette aide couvre la période du 1er au 15 novembre et s’inscrit dans les mesures destinées à limiter l’impact des variations des prix des carburants sur le secteur. Cette décision intervient au lendemain d’une réunion gouvernementale présidée par la Cheffe du Gouvernement, Fatima-Zahra El Mansouri, consacrée à l’examen de la conjoncture économique nationale, au suivi du pouvoir d’achat des citoyens et à l’effet des fluctuations des prix sur le marché national comme sur les conditions de vie des ménages. Dans une déclaration à Hespress ce mercredi, Abdessamad Kayouh a expliqué que la poursuite de ce dispositif exceptionnel vise à « protéger le pouvoir d’achat des citoyens et garantir la stabilité des marchés », alors que la volatilité des cours des carburants pèse sur les coûts du transport. Sur le plan pratique, l’inscription des professionnels à ce nouveau soutien ouvrira le 10 novembre, avant le versement des sommes aux transporteurs. L’aide afférente à la période précédente sera, elle aussi, débloquée dans les meilleurs délais, a assuré le ministre. Il a également dressé un bilan chiffré de l’opération. Depuis le lancement du soutien exceptionnel, 11 milliards de dirhams, soit plus d’un milliard de dollars, ont été versés aux professionnels du transport, dont environ 2,5 milliards de dirhams pour la seule année 2026. Quant au choix d’une périodicité semi-mensuelle, Abdessamad Kayouh l’a rattaché au mode de fixation des prix du gasoil dans les stations-service, qui repose sur deux périodes par mois : la première court du 1er au milieu du mois, la seconde du 15 jusqu’à la fin du mois. Pour le transport de voyageurs, les autocars assurant les liaisons interurbaines percevront 5 600 dirhams au titre de la période, contre 4 960 dirhams pour les bus du transport public urbain. Les véhicules de transport touristique bénéficient de montants échelonnés selon leur catégorie : 2 240 dirhams pour la première, 1 220 dirhams pour la deuxième et 800 dirhams pour la troisième. Les petits taxis recevront 1 280 dirhams, les grands taxis 1 760 dirhams, tandis que les véhicules de transport mixte en milieu rural toucheront 1 440 dirhams. Du côté du transport de marchandises, les tracteurs routiers se voient allouer 4 800 dirhams. Pour le transport de marchandises pour compte d’autrui, le montant varie selon la charge : 2 080 dirhams pour les camions dont le tonnage dépasse 3,5 tonnes sans atteindre 14 tonnes, 2 720 dirhams pour la deuxième catégorie et 3 360 dirhams pour les véhicules excédant 19 tonnes. Le dispositif englobe aussi le transport de personnel pour compte d’autrui, avec 960 dirhams par véhicule. Les véhicules de remorquage et d’assistance routière, communément appelés « dépannage », ainsi que ceux du transport scolaire pour compte d’autrui, percevront chacun 800 dirhams. Les services du ministère, à l’échelon central comme au niveau des directions régionales et provinciales, continuent par ailleurs d’accompagner les professionnels et de traiter les difficultés rencontrées lors de l’accès à la plateforme numérique d’inscription, tout en suivant le versement de l’aide aux différentes catégories bénéficiaires. The post Transport routier : nouvelle aide de 400 millions de DH appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Burkina Faso : Le président Assimi Goïta attendu à Ouagadougou ce jeudi pour une visite d’amitié et de travail
items.description: Le président de la Transition du Mali, le général d'armée Assimi Goïta, est annoncé à Ouagadougou le jeudi 5 novembre 2026 pour une visite d'amitié et de travail. Ce déplacement intervient quelques jours après sa participation au troisième Sommet Russie-Afrique, tenu à Moscou les 28 et 29 octobre derniers. Le Burkina Faso s'apprête à accueillir le chef de l'État malien. Le général d'armée Assimi Goïta est attendu dans la capitale burkinabè, ce jeudi 5 novembre 2026, dans le cadre d'une visite d'amitié et de travail, selon une information rapportée par l'Agence d'information du Burkina (AIB). Cette visite intervient après une séquence diplomatique marquée par la participation du dirigeant malien au troisième Sommet Russie-Afrique, organisé les 28 et 29 octobre 2026 à Moscou. À l'issue de cette rencontre internationale, Assimi Goïta avait regagné Bamako dans la matinée du dimanche 1er novembre. Son déplacement au Burkina Faso s'inscrit dans le contexte des relations de coopération entre les deux pays, membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES), aux côtés du Niger. La coopération entre les deux pays au cœur des échanges Cette rencontre devrait offrir aux deux chefs d'État l'occasion d'échanger sur les relations bilatérales et les enjeux communs auxquels leurs pays sont confrontés. Les questions sécuritaires, la coopération économique et le renforcement de la concertation au sein de l'AES constituent notamment des sujets d'intérêt dans les relations entre Ouagadougou et Bamako. Pour rappel, Assimi Goïta avait déjà effectué une visite d'amitié et de travail au Burkina Faso le 25 juin 2024. Il avait alors rencontré le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré pour des échanges portant notamment sur la lutte contre le terrorisme, le développement socioéconomique et la souveraineté des États sahéliens. Cette nouvelle visite annoncée intervient ainsi dans un contexte de poursuite des échanges entre les autorités burkinabè et maliennes. items.title: Orpailleurs burkinabè expulsés de Guinée : A Ouagadougou, les transporteurs se mobilisent aux côtés des autorités pour leur rapatriement
items.description: Environ 200 cars sont mobilisés à Ouagadougou pour rapatrier les compatriotes expulsés de Guinée. Si plusieurs cars ont bougé hier, une trentaine de cars étaient positionnés à la place de la Révolution, à Ouagadougou, ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026. Ces véhicules s'apprêtent à prendre la route pour aller chercher les Burkinabè expulsés des sites d'orpaillage en Guinée et faciliter leur retour au pays. Constat sur cette mobilisation. Depuis 2 heures du matin, ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, de nombreux cars appartenant à différentes compagnies de transport rallient la place de la Révolution, à Ouagadougou. Le ballet incessant des véhicules s'est poursuivi jusqu'à notre arrivée sur ce site de regroupement, d'où ils doivent prendre la direction de la frontière entre le Mali et la Guinée pour ramener nos compatriotes. À 11 heures, une trentaine de cars étaient déjà stationnés, en attente du départ. À leurs côtés, quelques convoyeurs piaffaient d'impatience à l'idée de partir à la rencontre de leurs compatriotes. « Nous sommes là depuis 2 heures du matin à la place de la Révolution pour aller à la recherche de nos frères », confie Moussa Zoromé, convoyeur à la Société de transport Ousmane et fils (STROF) International. En attendant le départ, ses confrères et lui prennent des clichés des véhicules et des différentes compagnies qui rallient progressivement le site. Moussa Zoromé, convoyeur à la Société de transport Ousmane et fils (STROF) International Antoine Kaboré, vice-président national de la Faîtière unique des transporteurs routiers du Burkina, est également à pied d'œuvre sous un soleil de plomb. Un calepin à la main, il enregistre chaque car qui rejoint le site. Pendant qu'il note le flux des véhicules, son téléphone ne cesse de sonner. « Ce sont des transporteurs qui veulent aussi envoyer des cars. Il y a un véritable engouement depuis hier », nous explique-t-il après avoir raccroché. La veille, confie-t-il, plus de quarante cars ont déjà pris la route. Une cinquantaine d'autres véhicules devraient également prendre le départ ce mercredi, ajoute-t-il. « Avec le gouvernement, les transporteurs se sont mobilisés comme un seul homme pour accompagner le président du Faso dans ses actions. Depuis que les événements se sont passés, on a senti un gouvernement au cœur de la population, qui travaille à ce que nos concitoyens rentrent avec dignité », fait-il savoir. Pour le vice-président national de la Faîtière unique des transporteurs routiers du Burkina, cette mobilisation dépasse les frontières de Ouagadougou. À Bobo-Dioulasso, deuxième grande ville du Burkina Faso, l'engouement est également au rendez-vous. L'objectif, souligne-t-il, est de préserver la dignité des Burkinabè partout où ils se trouvent. Selon lui, environ 200 cars ont été mobilisés depuis hier pour la cause. Deux heures après notre passage, soit à 14h, les cars avaient déjà bougé. Antoine Kaboré, vice-président national de la Faîtière unique des transporteurs routiers du Burkina, a salué la solidarité nationale autour de cette cause Des vivres également mobilisés Aux côtés des transporteurs, le ministère de l'Action humanitaire apporte également sa contribution à cette opération de solidarité. Sur le site de la place de la Révolution, de jeunes manutentionnaires déchargent un camion-benne rempli de sacs de riz. « C'est le ministère de l'Action humanitaire. Ce sont des vivres destinés à nos compatriotes qui arrivent. Le ministère veille toujours à ce que les gens puissent avoir de quoi manger », explique Antoine Kaboré. Lire aussi : Expulsion de Burkinabè de Guinée Conakry : Le gouvernement prend des mesures pour organiser leur retour dans « la dignité et la décence » Après la place de la Révolution, nous nous sommes rendus à la rencontre des responsables de certaines compagnies de transport. Mais les différents responsables n'ont pas souhaité s'exprimer. En effet, une délégation gouvernementale doit se rendre au Mali ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 afin d'apporter une assistance aux ressortissants burkinabè en situation de détresse et de faciliter leur retour au pays dans « la dignité et la décence ». Ces cars sont prêts pour le départ Face à cette situation, les autorités burkinabè ont appelé les populations au calme et à la retenue. Elles les ont également invitées à faire preuve de vigilance face aux tentatives de manipulation et de désinformation. Pour rappel, plusieurs ressortissants burkinabè pratiquant l'orpaillage artisanal sur le territoire guinéen ont été expulsés de ce pays. Serge Ika Ki Lefaso.net

items.title: LDC : Serhou Guirassy sort sur blessure et inquiète avant la double confrontation face à l’Érythrée
items.description: C'est probablement un coup dur pour la Guinée à quelques jours de sa double confrontation face à l’Érythrée. Serhou Guirassy a été contraint de quitter ses coéquipiers sur blessure, ce mercredi, lors de la rencontre entre le Borussia Dortmund et le Bétis Séville, comptant pour la phase de ligue de la Ligue des champions. Une situation qui suscite des inquiétudes quant à sa disponibilité pour les prochaines échéances du Syli national. Titulaire au coup d’envoi de cette rencontre européenne, l’attaquant international guinéen n’aura disputé que 34 minutes avant de céder sa place à la suite d’une blessure. Une sortie prématurée qui pourrait constituer un sérieux coup dur pour la sélection guinéenne, à l’approche de ses deux prochains rendez-vous internationaux. Pour l’heure, aucune communication officielle n’a été faite sur la nature exacte de la blessure de l’avant-centre du Borussia Dortmund, encore moins sur la durée de son éventuelle indisponibilité. Il est donc trop tôt pour se prononcer sur sa participation à la prochaine fenêtre internationale. Cette situation intervient à quelques jours de la double confrontation entre la Guinée et l’Érythrée, prévue les 12 et 16 novembre prochains, dans le cadre des 3e et 4e journées des éliminatoires de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2027. Pièce maîtresse du dispositif offensif de Paulo Duarte, Serhou Guirassy représente l'un des atouts majeurs du Syli national dans cette campagne qualificative. Son éventuelle absence serait ainsi un handicap pour la sélection guinéenne, qui ambitionne de faire le plein de points face à l’Érythrée. Les prochaines heures devraient permettre d’en savoir plus sur la gravité de cette blessure et les chances de voir Guirassy répondre présent pour ces deux rencontres décisives. items.title: Bob Dylan Meets With Pope Leo
Revenge of the White Working Class
items.description: L ast night, in the streets of Austin, Democrats honked their horns and hung out their windows, like it was V-E Day. In the nation’s capital, they blasted “Party in the U.S.A.” near the White House. But in southeast Iowa, the blue revolution came quietly. The Democrats of Des Moines County—a place that does not actually contain the state capital, but a small, industrial river city and rural areas along the Mississippi—have not come to associate Election Night with joy. The half dozen white-haired Iowans at the Burlington office’s “watch party” were blinking in disbelief at the TV as MS NOW election alerts flashed across the screen. Their party had retaken the governorship of Ohio—and somehow won a Senate seat in South Carolina? Texas was within reach. So, it seemed, was Kansas? “This might be a very big night,” Tom Courtney, a 79-year-old former state senator and former leader of the county party, told me, in what was already sounding like a colossal understatement. Iowa’s results had yet to come in. He and the other Democrats in the room seemed to be experiencing happiness only distantly, like birdsong from deep within a dark wood. This county, which had elected Barack Obama by about 23 points in 2008, was one of 31 Iowa counties that swung to Donald Trump in 2016. Two years ago, Trump won Des Moines County by 15 points, and Democrats began speaking of the “river counties” in the past tense—pieces of Iowa’s blue wall, lost forever. Courtney was on the phone. He paced the office, passing lawn signs, a cooling pot of chili, and the final slices of a Casey’s taco pizza. Then, suddenly, gasps. The countywide results were in, and a map of election results showed Des Moines County faintly—yet undeniably—blue. The county’s voters had opted to send a Democrat to the state house and another to the U.S. House; they’d also voted to make Rob Sand the state’s first Democratic governor elected in 20 years. “Did you hear that?” Courtney asked me, from across the room. By the end of the night, Iowa would also send Josh Turek to the Senate, plus three Democrats to the House. Kansas would send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since the invention of beer in a can. In Ohio, the party would send Sherrod Brown back to Congress, and Amy Acton to the governor’s mansion. At the office in Des Moines County, Courtney’s wife, Nancy, emerged from the office kitchen with several plastic cups full of room-temperature peppermint schnapps. “We did good,” she told the small group of people, which, despite the cavalcade of thrilling news, was maintaining a measured, midwestern composure. A fortunate combination of variables had put Iowa, and the rest of the Midwest, back on the map for Democrats. The next big challenge for the party will be keeping it there. W ar. Tariffs. Gas prices. It’s all I heard at the polls yesterday morning in Iowa, where, like pretty much everywhere else, the midterm elections were a referendum on choices made by President Trump. Even loyal Republicans I spoke with at the polls seemed bummed to be voting for the GOP. “Somebody’s gotta do it,” one man told me outside Burlington’s First Church of Nazarene when I asked how he felt about Republican leadership. Later, a woman on the other side of town told me she was eating mostly toast and tacos to save money. She’d still submitted an all-Republican ticket, she said. “But I didn’t want to vote for any of them.” Still, to have a night like last night, Democrats needed more than bad atmospheric conditions for Republicans: They needed good candidates. And where it mattered most, they had them. In Iowa, Democrats ran Sand, a centrist who has emphasized frugality and promised to take on corruption. “Right person, right message, right place, right time,” Sandy Dockendorff, a longtime Democratic activist in Des Moines County, told me. Her party also had Turek, a four-time U.S. Paralympian whose compelling backstory and commitment to moderation proved enough to defeat Ashley Hinson, widely considered to be the star Republican recruit of the cycle. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Jon Husted, despite the latter’s allegedly fantastic posterior . And in Kansas, Democrats managed to get Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who until recently was a Republican, at the top of the slate. It helped that Hamilton’s opponent, the incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, was impressively weak. “In a shitty environment, one way you don’t win races is to combine shitty candidates running shitty campaigns,” a senior—and very bitter—GOP strategist involved in multiple Senate races, said. [ Read: Who thought this ad was a good idea? ] The lesson, according to national Democrats, is clear: The winning candidates were “comfortable being a different type of Democrat,” the party strategist Lis Smith told me in a text. Those candidates had worked hard to persuade independents and Republicans, even if “it didn’t always earn them fans online.” Perhaps Smith is referring, in part, to the way that Sand and Turek handled some of the most contentious issues facing the party. Both candidates, for example, ditched the party line to say that transgender girls should not play in girls sports. Last week, Turek released an ad about it that had sent many Democrats sputtering . He won anyway. “Democrats need to get better at winning rural voters,” Adam Jentleson, president of the center-left think tank Searchlight Institute, told me. “Iowa is the testing ground, and Sand and Turek are the models.” [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Last night, every county in both Kansas and Iowa moved left. Dockendorff, the longtime Des Moines County activist, had told me over coffee yesterday morning that something like this would happen. (I trusted her because, in 2020, she had been the Cassandra of the caucuses, warning me —correctly—that Iowa’s vaunted nominating contest was likely to devolve into chaos.) “Iowa is turning back to purple,” she said. A year ago, or maybe less, Democratic activists had started filling chairs at county party meetings again. Some young people, too. Energy wise, she said, “there is no comparison to 2018.” This was much, much bigger. River towns, like Burlington, where the decline of unions had hollowed out the party, were showing some potential for Democrats once more. “I hear dissatisfaction from voters here,” she said. “People trusted Trump to do . He hasn’t done .” This assessment inspired another warning from Dockendorff—for Democrats both in and outside of Iowa. “This is not a coronation of the Democratic Party,” she said. It is an expression of frustration from voters looking for something different. “Our problem will be creating that something different.” Last night, for example, Iowans passed a constitutional amendment that will make it more difficult to raise income taxes, which might make it harder for Iowa’s new leaders to address the state’s budget shortfall. And voters in Des Moines County and others that flipped are not suddenly committed Democrats. National Democrats have been warning for months that a significant win in November would be overinterpreted by party activists and leaders, who would assume that voters were in love with their message, rather than simply sick of the president’s antics. The Democratic Party remains thoroughly unpopular. With Trump repudiated , albeit not totally in the rearview mirror, Democrats now have the challenge of presenting an affirmative vision for the country. How will they lower gas prices, or the price of milk? How will they talk about transgender issues as a party? Or immigration? Now, Dockendorff said, “the internecine war begins.” [ Read: The Democratic base is angry ] Signs of the coming conflict were on display last night at the watch party in Des Moines County. Sometime after the announcement that Florida Democrats had broken the state’s Republican supermajority but before the schnapps, Ben Diewold, a co-leader of the group, said he hoped that the Democrats wouldn’t try to impeach Trump again. “All that’s gonna do is invigorate MAGA,” he said. “Let Trump fade away.” Nancy didn’t agree. “He needs to be accountable to all that he’s done.” Soon, though, their conversation was interrupted. MS NOW was projecting that James Talarico had won in Texas. (“TalaFREAKO!” Diewold shouted.) And Rob Sand would lead Iowa. [ Read: How Texas turned blue ] “I’m glad I’m alive to see it,” Courtney said. He dictated a congratulations text and sent it to Sand. A few minutes later, a couple of the younger staffers, who’d come to work in Iowa from California and New Jersey, left to celebrate at a bar downtown. They asked Courtney to join them, but he declined. He wanted to keep watching. Madeleine Carlisle contributed reporting.

items.title: Google Won’t Give Schools the One Thing They Want
items.description: Over the past few years, Google’s low-priced laptops have become an AI Trojan horse in America’s schools. Students can use a school-issued Chromebook to automate much of their homework. Fire up the Gemini app, and Google’s chatbot will spit out a full essay about the meaning of The Giver . Type an algebra question into the Google search box, and an “AI Overview” will solve it for you. Ask a follow-up question, and the search box might give way to “AI Mode,” which turns the search engine into a full-on chatbot. Districts across the country give each student their own device, which typically comes equipped with a Google account and a suite of the company’s software. Over the past year, some of the country’s largest public-school districts, including Los Angeles and New York City, have passed policies limiting students’ screen time and banning generative-AI tools. But they hit an obstacle: Google didn’t offer schools a way to fully opt out of AI. Yesterday, the tech giant’s attempt to address the problem only made people madder. Google’s stand-alone Gemini chatbot will now be disabled by default for school accounts, the company announced . But Google quietly left out any option to turn off its most popular and widely used generative-AI features: those built into its search engine. In other words, the only way for schools to go AI-free is to cut off students’ access to Google Search, the world’s most popular website. Tech companies threatening to withdraw products rather than modify them has become part of Silicon Valley’s playbook. (Meta once responded to a Canadian law requiring the company to share revenue with news publishers by banning news articles from its platform altogether.) Online, the move drew outrage, including from congressional Democrats who will soon hold newfound legislative and subpoena powers. “Google is once again prioritizing profits over people,” Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut posted . “Clearly, the Tech Giant is more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.” Google contended that the anger was based on a misunderstanding. “Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less ,” the company posted on X, evincing a faith in the power of boldface font to get its message across. That much is true. Google has never offered schools an AI-free version of its search engine (though there is a “Web” tab that limits results to links). What was new in Google’s announcement was that both Gemini and Search will now be turned off by default, and schools will have the option to enable one or both. For schools that enable Search, the company is touting a new “guided learning” mode in its AI features that will prompt students to work through questions one step at a time, rather than simply giving them the answer. That could help address one of the biggest objections to Google’s AI search tools in the classroom, which is that they short-circuit the learning process. (A spokesperson for the company declined to comment beyond pointing me to its public statements.) [ Read: My son’s math homework is essentially just Pokémon ] Yet Google’s response to the blowback failed to address the aspect of its announcement that had upset people in the first place. The company wasn’t taking away any options that had existed before, but it also wasn’t providing the one option schools seemed to want most: a way to let students use Google Search without also enabling the AI bells and whistles. The unspoken logic behind the company’s stance is that, in some sense, all Search is AI search. AI Overviews and AI Mode launched in 2024 and 2025, respectively, but the company has been using large language models to help rank its search results since well before the arrival of ChatGPT. Google also used AI for years to help power the precursors to AI Overviews, including “featured snippets”—those bolded excerpts from web results that Google surfaced atop its list of links. So when Google says that opting out of AI entails opting out of Search, that’s technically true. Even so, there’s something obtuse about Google’s refusal to acknowledge that consumers—and schools especially—might reasonably draw a distinction between LLMs that help power search results and LLMs that generate answers themselves. Parents and teachers mostly don’t object to Google using AI to decide which webpages to link to when students ask a question (though there is a case to be made that the company’s opaque ranking process has always deserved more scrutiny than it’s received). They object to turning Google into an instant-answer machine—and an error-prone one, at that. They object to students being conditioned to delegate their critical-thinking and source-evaluation skills to a machine. And they object to infusing the same site that indexes the world’s online information with a chatbot that can function as an ersatz friend or dispense personal advice to impressionable children. Which brings us to the business logic underlying Google’s stubborn stance. The company built its empire around a search tool that offered the shortest path between a user’s question and the information they were seeking. For years, that mostly meant refining its algorithm to downgrade spammy sites in its results. Then came ChatGPT, which promised to answer just about anything a user could ask, dispensing with the list of links altogether. OpenAI claimed this week that ChatGPT now handles about one-fifth as many search queries as Google. Chatbots are the most significant threat to Google’s core business that the search giant has ever faced. Its response has been to morph Search into an AI-answer tool in its own right. A few discontented users have dropped Google for niche alternatives such as DuckDuckGo, the privacy-focused search engine that now touts AI-free search as a selling point. Kamyl Bazbaz, a DuckDuckGo spokesperson, told me that usage of the company’s “No-AI” search option is up 30 percent since September. The company is now looking for ways to make it easier for schools that opt out of Google Search to switch their default search engine, he added. But Google seems to be betting that convenience will win out over qualms about generative AI. That bet could easily pay off, given how accustomed students already are to the tools Google has provided them with. While researching this story, I asked Google for data on how many Chromebooks are in U.S. schools. The site responded with an AI Overview confidently asserting that 93 percent of U.S. school districts plan to purchase Chromebooks. In small print, the overview cited one source for that figure: an article from a website called commandlinux.com. Skeptical, I did what fewer and fewer Google users are doing these days: I clicked on the link. The article, which appeared to be AI-written, offers no methodology or original source for any of the figures it provides. I took those extra steps because I’m a professional journalist who covers AI and its limitations for a living, and because my own schooling trained me to seek out original sources and evaluate their credibility. Had I grown up with AI search, as today’s kids do, I doubt I would have thought to question the number that Google handed me.

items.description: Les éléments de la brigade régionale de lutte contre les stupéfiants de Sousse ont réussi un coup de filet en saisissant environ 250 grammes de résine de cannabis, ainsi qu'une quantité de comprimés psychotropes. Lors de cette intervention, une somme d'argent et une balance de précision ont également été confisquées, indique Mosaïque FM ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, en citant une source proche du dossier. L'opération sécuritaire, menée dans le quartier Laouina à Sousse, a permis l'interpellation de trois individus, dont un ressortissant d'un pays d'Afrique subsaharienne. Après consultation du ministère public, les dealers ont été placés en garde à vue et l'enquête se poursuit. Y. N. items.title: Le souverain marocain ordonne au gouvernement la prise en charge du processus de retrait de la MINURSO du pays
items.description: Le souverain marocain Mohammed VI a chargé le ministère de l'Intérieur de coordonner les procédures de liquidation et de retrait de la Mission des Nations unies (MINURSO), après que le Conseil de sécurité de l'ONU ait décidé, lors de sa réunion du 30 octobre, de ne pas renouveler son mandat. Le communiqué indique que le souverain marocain a donné instruction au « Bureau de coordination avec la MINURSO », rattaché au ministère de l’Intérieur, de prendre en charge le suivi du processus de retrait de la mission et de coordonner les mesures y afférentes avec les Nations unies, afin d’en garantir le bon déroulement. Il a ajouté que le roi avait souligné, lors d’une réunion au palais royal de Rabat, la nécessité de suivre l’évolution du dossier du Sahara à différents niveaux et de poursuivre les projets de développement dans les provinces du sud, tout en insistant sur l’engagement du Maroc à respecter le cessez-le-feu, malgré la fin du mandat de la mission onusienne. Le Maroc a réaffirmé son attachement à la proposition d’autonomie, considérée, selon le communiqué, comme la seule solution politique au conflit, en rappelant la reconnaissance par des pays amis et frères de sa souveraineté sur le Sahara. La réunion a rassemblé la cheffe du gouvernement Fatima Zahra Mansouri, le conseiller du roi Fouad Ali El Himma, le ministre de l’Intérieur Abdelouafi Laftit et l’inspecteur général des Forces armées royales Mohamed Bariz.
