items.title: Mamadou Moustapha Ba, le souvenir d’un technocrate au service de l’État
items.description: Deux ans après sa disparition le 4 novembre 2024 en France, à l’âge de 59 ans , Mamadou Moustapha Ba reste associé à une longue carrière consacrée aux finances publiques Haut fonctionnaire devenu ministre sous le régime de Macky Sall, cet homme de dossiers a marqué l’administration financière par son expertise et sa discrétion. Né le 6 août 1965 à Nioro du Rip, dans la région de Kaolack, Mamadou Moustapha Ba a très tôt emprunté la voie de l'excellence scolaire. Après un baccalauréat obtenu au Prytanée militaire de Saint-Louis, il poursuit ses études à l’École nationale d’économie appliquée (ENEA) de Dakar, dont il sort diplômé en 1991. Désireux d'approfondir ses connaissances, il poursuit son cursus en Belgique, où il décroche un diplôme en politique de développement ainsi qu’un master en gestion et administration publique à l’Université d’Anvers. Son parcours professionnel prend véritablement forme au début des années 1990. En 1992, il intègre le ministère de l’Économie et des Finances, où il construit progressivement sa réputation de technicien maîtrisant les rouages de l’administration financière. Il rejoint ensuite la Direction de la coopération économique et financière au début des années 2000. En 2007, il en devient directeur adjoint, avant d'en prendre la tête en mai 2012. Il occupe cette fonction jusqu'en octobre 2014. Il poursuit ensuite son ascension au sein de l'administration financière et devient directeur général du Budget, un poste stratégique qu'il occupe pendant plusieurs années. Le 17 septembre 2022 marque un tournant dans sa carrière. Le président Macky Sall le nomme ministre des Finances et du Budget, dans le gouvernement dirigé par Amadou Ba. Il hérite ainsi d'un portefeuille stratégique, au cœur de la conduite des politiques économiques et budgétaires du pays. Il restera à ce poste jusqu'en avril 2024, devenant le dernier ministre des Finances et du Budget du régime de Macky Sall. Mais son parcours s'interrompt brutalement quelques mois après son départ du gouvernement. Le 04 novembre 2024, Mamadou Moustapha Ba décède à Paris, à l'âge de 59 ans. Si l'annonce officielle de sa disparition intervient le 4 novembre, les circonstances de sa mort vont rapidement susciter de nombreuses interrogations. En France, les investigations privilégient la thèse du suicide, des éléments issus de la vidéosurveillance du métro parisien ayant été évoqués par la presse. Au Sénégal, le procureur de la République ordonne, le 10 novembre, l'ouverture d'une enquête après que les résultats de l'autopsie ont fait état d'éléments attestant d'une mort non naturelle. La levée du corps et l'inhumation, initialement prévues à cette période, sont alors reportées. L'ancien ministre sera finalement inhumé le 13 novembre 2024 au cimetière Nouroulaye de Nioro du Rip, sa ville natale. Une foule composée de membres de sa famille, de responsables politiques, d'anciens collaborateurs et de personnalités administratives et religieuses lui rend un dernier hommage. Plusieurs témoignages saluent alors son professionnalisme, sa disponibilité, son sens du dialogue et son engagement au service de l'État. Deux ans après sa disparition, Mamadou Moustapha Ba demeure une figure marquante de l'administration financière sénégalaise. Derrière le ministre, il y avait surtout un haut fonctionnaire qui aura consacré plus de trois décennies de sa vie professionnelle aux finances publiques. Un parcours dont le souvenir reste attaché aux grandes responsabilités qu'il a exercées au service de son pays. A.N

items.title: Yasmina Khadra à TSA : « Ce qui arrive au peuple palestinien est abominable »
items.description: En marge de la 29ᵉ édition du Salon international d’Alger (SILA 2026) auquel il participe à l’occasion de la parution de son tout nouveau roman Le prieur de Bethléem (Casbah Editions) , Yasmina Khadra s’est confié à TSA. De la tragédie en Palestine occupée au piège du fanatisme en Israël, en passant par son boycott en France et la montée de l'extrême droite, le célèbre écrivain algérien s'exprime sans concession. TSA : Dans votre nouveau roman ‘Le prieur de Bethléem’, vous abordez le drame que vit le peuple palestinien, à travers l’histoire d’un éditeur parisien kidnappé par un moine palestinien, dont le manuscrit a été rejeté. Pourriez-vous nous en dire plus ? Yasmina Khadra : Est-ce qu’on peut appeler ça un drame ? C’est encore plus terrible, il faut trouver un néologisme pour vraiment expliquer ce qui se passe dans ce pays martyrisé. C’est abominable, c’est inacceptable, il n’y a pas de vocable pour parler de cette chose horrible qui arrive au peuple palestinien. Ce roman est aussi une fresque sur la déshumanisation. Comment préserver son humanité lorsque la violence est partout ? Yasmina Khadra : Ce n’est pas la violence qui nous déshumanise, c’est le fanatisme. On peut être violent, avoir des regrets et demander pardon. Mais là où c’est impossible d’accéder à quelques scrupules ou à quelques raisonnements, c’est dans le fanatisme. En Israël, il y a des gens qui sont complètement fanatisés, et quand on est fanatique, on est dépossédé de sa propre âme, de soi-même et on devient un outil d’extermination. On devient de l’antimatière : tout ce qu’on touche disparaît. Que pensez-vous des jeunes écrivains algériens qui émergent ? Quel conseil pouvez-vous leur donner ? Yasmina Khadra : Il y a beaucoup de jeunes qui écrivent dans les trois langues : tamazight, arabe et français, c’est merveilleux ! Le conseil que je me permets de leur donner, c’est de s’accrocher à cette vocation parce qu’elle est livrée à pas mal d’indifférences et de rejets. Nos écrivains, comme nos artistes, ne sont pas encouragés dans ce pays. Quand on écrit, on s’épuise, on se donne à fond, on a de l’espoir et puis d’un seul coup, il n’y a pas de répondant, il n’y a pas un espace où on peut être fiers de ce qu’on a écrit. Parfois, on est confrontés à de l’incompréhension, de la censure. Le conseil que je leur donne, c’est de continuer à écrire malgré tout et de ne rien attendre des autres. Vous dites que vous avez été exclu et boycotté en France. Pourquoi ce sentiment ? Yasmina Khadra : Ce n’est pas un sentiment, c’est un constat. Je ne me plains pas, je dénonce seulement une attitude incompréhensible pour le commun des mortels, mais qui a certainement un sens bien établi par des gens, par des réseaux, par des lobbies. C’est une vérité, ça crève les yeux. Depuis 2008, je suis exclu par toutes les institutions et tous les jurys littéraires. Pourtant, je n’écris pas n’importe quoi, chaque année, j’écris l’un des meilleurs, sinon le meilleur livre de l’année. En France, on me dit Monsieur Khadra, quand on vous lit, on a du mal à lire les autres ! Et peut-être que c’est ça qui m’exclut. Allez-vous rester dans une France gouvernée par l’extrême droite qui est plus que jamais proche du pouvoir ? Yasmina Khadra : Moi, je vis en Algérie, j’y suis pendant 8 à 9 mois. Je me rends en France uniquement à l’occasion de la sortie d’un nouveau livre ou lorsque j’ai une tournée. Cette France, moi, ne m’effraie pas. J’ai six millions de lecteurs en France, cela prouve que la France n’est pas raciste. Certes, il y a des racistes en France, l’extrême droite est un peu partout. C’est un peu tout l’Occident qui est en train de sombrer dans cette mouvance dévastatrice qui va finir par le détruire. Il y a beaucoup de Français qui sont contre l’extrême droite et surtout la jeunesse. La preuve, dans les récentes manifestations, on a vu tous ces jeunes qui sont absolument hostiles à ces dérives qui ne sont que des vocations carriéristes. L’extrême droite n’a pas de projet de société. Quand on entend un prétendant à la présidentielle dire : ‘Moi, mon travail c’est de supprimer wech et wallah’, qu’est-ce que cela va changer dans la vie et le pouvoir d’achat des Français ? Rien. Ce sont des gens qui sont dans une sorte d’euphorie, fascinés par leur propre violence et qui croient faire peur. Moi, je ne crains pas ces gens-là et personne ne devrait avoir peur de ces gens-là ! L’algérophobie est-elle réelle en France ? Yasmina Khadra : L’algérophobie n’existe pas en France. Il y a une paranoïa qui est véhiculée par les médias qui sont à la solde de certains lobbies et réseaux, mais les Français sont un peuple très éveillé et très éclairé. Il y a une mouvance avec des gens comme Éric Zemmour, Jordan Bardella ou Marion Maréchal qui ne savent pas ce qu’ils font ou qu’ils veulent faire du tort à la France et non aux Maghrébins. Ce sont des mouvements extrémistes, racistes, et c’est leur vocation. J’espère que les Français sont sur leurs gardes. J’interviens toujours dans ce genre de débats pour essayer de mobiliser les Français contre cette mouvance qui est un véritable péril pour le devenir de la France. L’article Yasmina Khadra à TSA : « Ce qui arrive au peuple palestinien est abominable » est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: $500 Million Bought Elon Nothing
items.description: Here are a few things $474 million can cover: roughly 77 million Big Macs, about 12,814 Tesla Model 3s, or approximately 2,724 years of a U.S. senator’s average salary. If you’re Elon Musk, it could also buy you one deeply disappointing evening in November. This year, Musk became the single largest non-candidate donor in any election cycle ever. His contributions to campaigns and organizations account for about one-quarter of all campaign donations Republicans received in 2026. More than $168 million of that money went to super PACs supporting the Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who lost yesterday to James Talarico, the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in Texas in 38 years. Musk gave $216 million to his own political action committee, America PAC, much of that going toward canvassing operations and advertising. Other donations went to either individual Republican candidates or organizations at both state and federal levels. In almost every instance, that money failed to buy the richest man in the world the results he wanted. [ Read: You can believe everything ] What does this mean for Musk? One could see it as a repudiation of the near trillionaire—a suggestion that he and the causes he stands for have become a toxic political influence. Though he was helpful in Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign, he has fumbled politically over the past two years, including with his disastrous run advising the Department of Government Efficiency. In 2025, he backed a failed state-supreme-court campaign in Wisconsin. Musk’s money in Paxton’s race may have backfired, signaling to Texans that a tech oligarch was trying to buy an election. At the very least, Musk’s influence seems to have galvanized Talarico. He made Musk and other rich donors a centerpiece of his campaign. During his victory speech last night, Talarico said the state sent a message to “every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor,” and “to the people at the top: We will not be conquered.” Musk was just the most prominent member of an entourage of Silicon Valley executives and investors who have enthusiastically supported Trump in his second term. In Trump and the MAGA movement, this Tech Right coalition saw opportunities for favorable legislation on issues such as crypto and little to no regulation on AI buildout and safety. Culturally, MAGA offered this cohort a permission structure for loud and proud anti-wokeness. Impressed by their money and perceived power, Trump let Silicon Valley leaders into government operations, making them czars or lieutenant colonels in the Army . Through DOGE, Musk and other unelected tech workers briefly took control of government agencies, data, and personnel management in an unprecedented bureaucratic coup. All of this seems to have rubbed many Americans the wrong way. Yesterday, the country voted in opposition to nearly every data-center ballot initiative and pro-data-center candidate. A majority of Americans in exit polls expressed deep concern about government corruption and also artificial intelligence. This election cycle, Musk appeared to represent almost every faction America has indicated that it is tired of right now. He is the oligarch class, data centers and AI, MAGA politics and cronyism all rolled into one man. Now Musk and the tech leaders will have to recalibrate their politics for a Congress that may be actively hostile to their interests. Perhaps it’s already started; Musk, who just a few weeks ago threatened retribution if Democrats sought to investigate him, deleted his X post saying “Vote red today!” after results came in on yesterday evening. From another angle, you could interpret the results as a refreshing example that massive influxes of donor money have diminishing returns—especially during midterm elections for a deeply unpopular administration and Congress. It’s possible that all the money in the world may not have been enough to help a candidate as deeply flawed as Paxton. Whatever your spin, it seems that Musk’s historic spending was a test—of Musk’s influence, his likability, him as a stand-in for the tech and AI industry, or simply the power of his net worth. On these fronts, the results are unflattering, even embarrassing. Back in May of 2025, Musk told Bloomberg that he was “going to do a lot less” political spending in the future. Clearly something changed. What did Musk think he was buying with the unprecedented contributions? There are the obvious financial motivations, especially for his spending in Texas—SpaceX, Tesla, and Musk are all based in the state. A Republican-controlled Congress might have also helped Musk’s businesses procure more government contracts; Republicans, taking cues from the Trump administration, would have been far less proactive in trying to regulate the AI industry, which would be ultimately beneficial to Musk’s interests. There’s the ideological motivation—Musk’s constant posting suggests that his right-wing, anti-immigration, and anti-woke politics are deeply held. Then there are the vanity and power dynamics: By almost single-handedly propping up Republicans this cycle, Musk would not only have ingratiated himself with GOP lawmakers but proved himself to be a kingmaker. Perhaps the biggest motivation for him supporting the GOP is his own potential vulnerability to government oversight and accountability. Many Democrats in Congress have explicitly raised the idea of opening investigations into Musk’s companies and contracts. There’s also the real possibility of a Democrat-controlled Congress investigating Musk’s time at DOGE. (This scenario recently prompted Trump to tell a podcaster that he would grant pardons to Musk and other DOGE associates.) For all these reasons, it matters that Musk’s money couldn’t buy him these elections. But still, one shouldn’t take Musk’s political defeat last night to suggest that he has lost his centrality in many of the world’s biggest and most consequential issues. Regardless of last night’s outcome, it should alarm you that Musk has so much money that he can independently stand up what Wired referred to as a “shadow Republican National Committee.” And that he can do this by spending about one-20th of 1 percent of his net worth. Put another way: Musk’s 2026 political donations are the equivalent of someone worth $1 million donating roughly $500. I’ve previously described Musk’s wealth as a chaos agent with no great comparison. To Musk’s credit, he’s used it shrewdly, rolling his companies into one another, which blurs their individual financials and increases their market value. He purchased Twitter, a politically influential platform that’s never had a good business model, and immediately alienated advertisers. At the time, I suggested that Musk was making a huge mistake, which was true in a business sense but ultimately irrelevant to Musk’s actual interests in transforming the platform into a political weapon. The bottom line didn’t matter; he could eat the losses or transfer them to another of his companies’ balance sheets. What mattered was Musk’s ability to influence and become one of the central figures in an important area of political and cultural discourse. The Twitter purchase was also helpful in establishing a narrative around Musk in certain right-wing spheres, where he became a hero as a free speech warrior eradicating the “woke mind virus.” In this way, Musk’s political donations echo his intent in purchasing Twitter. Donating to Republican candidates who used part of that money to buy ads is another way of influencing the discourse—what voters see when they turn on the TV or look at their phone or open their mailbox. Just as important to Musk is the message that money sends: the suggestion that he could purchase impunity for what amounts to pocket change. Or that even though he is a divisive figure, he is indispensable to the future of conservatism in the U.S. As we’ve learned over and over, Musk is a master of spectacle and getting people to believe and invest in the story he is telling about the future. Perhaps Musk saw his donations as a means of cementing himself as a main character in an election where he was not on the ballot. No one can know what the future holds for Musk. As other tech CEOs have already acknowledged, it might include constraints or potential regulation; Musk is already posting about the appeal of taking his data centers to space. But one way to look at last night’s results is that voters did what investors and many politicians have never been able to bring themselves to do: They rejected Musk’s story of himself as a larger-than-life figure who can use his wealth to turn his every whim into a reality.

items.title: 38 briefly detained in Karachi as police baton-charge protesters headed towards CM House
items.description: KARACHI: Thirty-eight people were released after brief detention on Wednesday as police used tear gas and batons against protesting teachers headed towards Chief Minister House from Karachi Press Club (KPC). Hundreds of teachers had gathered outside the press club at the call of the All Sindh Primary Teachers Association (ASPTA). They were headed towards CM House to present their demands that pertained to the service structure and called for delegating powers for transfers and postings to district officers. The protesters chanted slogans and attempted to move towards the CM House. However, when they arrived near Fawara Chowk, police baton-charged them and used tear gas shells to push them back toward the press club. Adjoining roads near the KPC were closed to traffic, according to a traffic police spokesperson. South Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Syed Asad Raza told Dawn that all detained teachers “have been released at night”, after he confirmed in earlier comments that 38 people were taken into custody. Speaking to Dawn earlier in the day, the DIG noted that a teachers’ organisation had announced a protest at the KPC, with a march planned toward the CM House. He said prior to the protest, the administration made concerted efforts to resolve the matter through negotiations and engaged officials from the education department to facilitate meaningful dialogue. The official said the protest leadership was categorically told that entry into the Red Zone — a term used to denote the area surrounding Governor House and Chief Minister House — would not be permitted. Nevertheless, the administration was directed to exhaust all available resources and make every effort to ensure a peaceful resolution through dialogue, he said. Raza alleged that around 3:15pm, the protesters turned “violent, abandoned the course of negotiations and forcibly started advancing towards the CM House.” He claimed that the protesting teachers “breached police barricades and resorted to pelting police personnel with stones, causing injuries to one official.” “Upon reaching and crossing Kabir Masjid on Governor House Road, the situation escalated, compelling police to resort to shelling to disperse the violent mob and restore order,” said the South police chief. He said during the operation, 38 protesters, including ASPTA President Ghulam Rasool Mahar and General Secretary Aijaz Ali Chandio, were taken into custody. Raza insisted that police took drastic action as the teachers tried to enter the Red Zone. Meanwhile, Rafiq Nizamani, the vice president of the teachers’ association, told Dawn that in 2021, the Sindh government had chalked out an “education policy” under which it was decided that teachers would not be promoted and they would remain in the same pay scale. He said they launched a protest against this “arbitrary” decision as others were being promoted, but not them. He said that at the time, the government had assured them that their demands would be addressed, but this did not happen. He said apart from the service structure, their other demands pertained to delegating the powers of posting primary teachers to district government officials. He said that they wanted recruitment and the transfer/posting of teachers to be delegated to district officials. According to Nizamani, as the protesters moved from KPC towards CM House, police resorted to tear gas and a baton charge. He claimed that two teachers were also injured. Nizamani said that they had decided to set up a protest camp outside the KPC for the fulfilment of their demands. He admitted that the education officials had approached them for talks, but said they considered it “delaying tactics” in view of their past unfulfilled promises and decided to hold a protest march.

items.title: Ouagadougou: 24 mois de prison ferme requis contre Me Ini Esther Doli pour diffamation présumée
items.description: Le parquet a requis, mercredi 4 novembre 2026, une peine de 24 mois d’emprisonnement ferme et une amende de 2 millions de F CFA ferme contre l’avocate Ini Esther Doli, poursuivie pour diffamation présumée envers la police municipale de Ouagadougou. L’affaire fait suite à des publications sur Facebook liées au déguerpissement du maquis Allah Ti Kouma, selon l’Agence d’information du Burkina (AIB). L’affaire a été portée devant le Tribunal de grande instance (TGI) Ouaga I à la suite d’une plainte de la commune de Ouagadougou. En cause, deux publications diffusées le 15 août 2026 sur la page Facebook de l’avocate, au lendemain de l’opération de déguerpissement du maquis Allah Ti Kouma, présenté comme un «haut lieu de prostitution». Dans l’une de ses publications, Me Ini Esther Doli aurait notamment écrit: «Si on fouille bien, on trouverait à coup sûr d’anciens clients ou des clients actuels parmi les prétendus lutteurs contre la prostitution». Des propos que la délégation spéciale de la commune de Ouagadougou a considérés comme une atteinte à l’honneur et à la considération des agents de la police municipale. Elle a en effet établi un rapprochement entre cette déclaration et l’opération de déguerpissement du maquis, intervenue le 14 août 2026 sur décision de justice. À la barre, l’avocate a toutefois rejeté toute intention de s’en prendre spécifiquement à la police municipale. Elle a soutenu que ses déclarations relevaient d’une réflexion générale sur les différents acteurs impliqués dans le phénomène de la prostitution. De son côté, la partie civile a demandé au tribunal de déclarer la prévenue coupable des faits qui lui sont reprochés et a réclamé un franc symbolique à titre de dommages et intérêts. La défense, quant à elle, a plaidé la relaxe. Elle a estimé que l’intention de nuire et le lien entre les propos incriminés et la police municipale n’étaient pas établis. Les avocats de la prévenue ont également jugé disproportionnées les réquisitions du parquet, faisant valoir que leur cliente avait supprimé les publications concernées et adressé une lettre d’excuses au président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune. L’affaire est désormais mise en délibéré. Le Tribunal de grande instance Ouaga I rendra sa décision le 25 novembre 2026, date à laquelle Me Ini Esther Doli sera fixée sur son sort. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Ouagadougou: 24 mois de prison ferme requis contre Me Ini Esther Doli pour diffamation présumée est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Can Democrats Hold Trump Accountable?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with a reminder on how hard President Trump has worked over the past two years to prevent free and fair elections in 2026. Then David is joined by Dave Rapallo, a former longtime staff director of the House Committee on Oversight and Reform, for a conversation on what tools Democrats in Congress would have to investigate President Trump, and how the president might respond. David and Dave discuss both the challenges and the opportunities for Congress ahead for reasserting the rule of law in America. Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of I, Robot by Isaac Asimov and its influence on today’s tech world. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show . I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Dave Rapallo, a professor at Georgetown Law Center and one of America’s leading experts on congressional investigations: what they can accomplish, what they cannot accomplish. And we’ll be talking about the challenges and opportunities in the Congress ahead for reasserting the rule of law in America. This week’s book is I, Robot by Isaac Asimov, which is—whether you notice it or not, whether you’ve read it or not—has become kind of a bible of the AI era, a book that obviously has influenced many of the most important people in the AI community and the AI tech world. But before either the dialogue with Dave Rapallo or the book discussion of I, Robot, some opening thoughts about the dramatic events that are coming our way in American politics. I am recording this monologue on Monday, November 2nd. You are watching it sometime after Wednesday, November 4th. So you will know, probably, or you are soon to know, the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections, and I don’t yet know them. But there’s something else that you know that I don’t know that may be even more important or at least as important as the outcome—and that is whether or not President Trump tried on voting day to manipulate the election result. I don’t know that yet. You know that story and all its drama. I hope for good news. I hope that everything I’m about to say is completely irrelevant, and that you are watching this knowing, Well, that went off not too badly under the circumstances. But it’s important to keep in mind, as we come to this vote, how hard President Trump has worked over the past two years to prevent a free and fair election from culminating on Tuesday. Now, let’s just go through the roster. And you will remember many of these details, but I don’t think you’ll remember all of them. First, President Trump encouraged his party at the state level to engage in redistricting in the middle of the decade. President Trump started that in July ’25 by asking Texas Republicans to redraw their congressional map to create more favorable districts for the party, even though there was no new census data to base that redrawing on. Now, it’s not that things like this have never happened before in American history. They have happened before. But in our times, in modern times, it’s basic good government that you do the census in a year ending with a zero. You do the redistricting in the year ending with a one. And then everyone lives under the same maps for the next decade. And while those maps have some politics in them, some effort to prevent racial abuse in them, basically you try to draw something that’s reasonably fair within the political context of each state. President Trump blew all of that up and started a redistricting war, Democrats against Republicans. At first, Republicans took the advantage; then the Democrats seized it back. In the middle of it, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in April of 2026 to gut most or all of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, to allow Republicans to engage on a new wave of gerrymandering—this quite racially motivated—to gain advantage for themselves. And while the first round of gerrymandering in 2025 probably broke even or ended a little bit in the Democrats’ favor, this second round has clearly worked in the Republicans’ favor, backed by the Supreme Court. Now, if so far you would say, This is ugly politics, but again, not completely unprecedented. But the other things that the president has tried to do by executive order—those really are unprecedented. In March of 2025, he issued an executive order that would have required documentary proof of citizenship to register and stop the counting of mail-in ballots that arrived after Election Day from being counted. And he did all this not through the law, not through the law of the states—who are the ultimate keepers of the election, right, according to the Constitution—but through presidential personal power. Now, a judge stopped this, so it didn’t happen. But President Trump did not give up. In March of ’26, he issued another executive order, this time directed to the Postal Service, to set up a system allowing it to block delivery of mail ballots to voters who weren’t on the list submitted in advance by state election officials. This, again, was a completely arbitrary action, personal power by the president. Again, stopped by the courts. But he kept at it, with executive order after executive order taking upon the president powers that the Constitution assigns to Congress and to the states. There were repeated attempts to seize information belonging to the states—either to reopen the 2020 election, but also to test whether federal law-enforcement personnel could be used during the 2026 election to disrupt and seize information from those votes. He demanded state voter rolls. He tried to set aside state ballots while voting was underway. Again and again and again, President Trump tried to interfere. Again and again, he was stopped by the courts. He’s lost many more fights than he’s won, and that’s reassuring. But the question you will know the answer to, and that I don’t, is whether President Trump, as of Monday, November 2nd, is out of tricks, or whether there’s something dark and nasty reserved to try on November 3rd. As we built toward January 6th, 2021, everybody could see that something was coming. But I don’t think anybody imagined what was coming: the actual attempt to invade Congress and disrupt an election count by force, with putting the lives of the speaker of the House and Trump’s own vice president at risk. No one anticipated just that, even though we could hear the momentum toward something bad. In this cycle, we also hear the momentum to something bad. I don’t know what that something is. You may know. Let’s hope it was nothing too terrible. Let’s hope it was defeated, as the preelection attempts were defeated. But if not, and if, as you watch this, you are dealing—and I am and my future self—are dealing with something nightmarish in America, let’s all hope that we can be strong through the next two years, as we’ve had to be strong through the past two years. And now, my dialogue with David Rapallo. [ Music ] Frum: Dave Rapallo is an associate professor of law at the Georgetown University Law Center. He spent 23 years in senior positions in Congress and the White House. For a decade, he was staff director of the House Oversight and Reform Committee. In President Obama’s first term, he was senior director and counsel for legislative oversight at the National Security Council. His academic work focuses on congressional investigative power, with special attention to the minority party’s tools. Dave Rapallo, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show. David Rapallo: Thanks for having me. Appreciate it. Frum: Just to make things transparent for our viewers and listeners, we are recording this discussion before the midterm elections of 2026—or, at any rate, before we know the outcome of the midterm elections of 2026. And we’ll be posting it after you, the viewer or listener, do know those outcomes. But for the purposes of today’s show, we are going to assume that there will be a change in the balance of power in at least one house of Congress, maybe two. And I’m going to ask Dave to explain to us what a new majority in either house can realistically do, and what it realistically cannot do, with the gavels of the chair of the majority power. So let me start with that. What should people not expect from a new majority by way of investigative power and constraint on presidential action? Rapallo: Well, thanks for having me. I really appreciate it. I think assuming, like you’re saying, that the Democrats have taken the House or the Senate or both, they’re going to have a steep road ahead in terms of enforcing subpoenas. There are legal enforcement methods; there are nonlegal enforcement methods. I think the challenges posed by the Trump administration in particular are unprecedented in terms of both the scale and the severity of those challenges. But I do think a Democratic majority, despite a steep climb in this area, can achieve significant goals if they plan ahead and they organize themselves, and they use the tools that they do have available in a smart way. Frum: So let’s start with the obstacles. When you were in the Obama administration, it probably did not occur to you that you had the option of simply, when you received a subpoena, simply crumpling it up, throwing it away, and ignoring it. Rapallo: No, not at all. Frum: But it turns out, that is an option. Rapallo: Yeah. In fact, we saw it during the first Trump administration, when I was still working as staff director on the House Oversight Committee. The president went out on the White House lawn and declared , “We’re fighting all the subpoenas.” There was no distinguishing what the subject matters were, whether there was an adequate privilege asserted. It was a blanket refusal to comply, and it didn’t have anything to do with the substance. He just declared that they were all partisan and therefore all invalid. And that is, constitutionally, just an unacceptable position. Frum: And people in the administration, likewise—or people who had been in the administration or in President Trump’s orbit—they also refused to comply. And in some cases, they served prison sentences because of their noncompliance. Rapallo: They did, yes, especially with respect to the January 6th investigation. Two of them were held in criminal contempt and did time. So in that case, there was a remedy. But of course, that was after President Trump had left office and we had a different president. Frum: Because you had a Justice Department that was willing to assist Congress in enforcing subpoenas. Rapallo: Exactly. Frum: So where you’re going to be, likely, in ’27 and ’28 is with a Justice Department that shares with the president the view the president doesn’t have to answer any questions. Rapallo: Correct. The president and a lot of administration officials, probably, will be their position. Frum: Let’s start by playing President Trump’s cards. So, you have an uncomfortable awareness that you’ve done a lot of things that might not look good if brought to light. In fact, won’t look good if brought to light. And some of them may even be illegal; some of them may be criminal. So you’re playing the cards to protect that. So let’s start by playing President Trump’s hand against Congress, and then let’s play Congress’s hand against President Trump. The Trump hand first. So, move one: Ignore subpoenas. Move two: Justice Department says We won’t help Congress enforce the subpoenas . What’s move three? Rapallo: Well, I think even before move one, I mean, typically—it’s important to say this—I think that a lot of requests from Congress traditionally had been voluntarily complied with. I mean, that was the norm. There was a famous memo during the Reagan presidency that says, We’re going to try and accommodate any congressional request to the extent that we can legally. And that’s what’s changed. Now there’s, I think, much more of an obstruction type of view. Now, I don’t think necessarily that’s going to be consistent throughout the entire administration. I think it’s one important thing—and I know we’re getting into the congressional side—but you’re going to be the last two years of an administration. A lot of the people in this administration may want to have jobs in the future. You also have the entire two-year Congress in the shadow of a presidential election. So those candidates on the Republican side who may currently be in the administration might have a different view than the president in terms of whether they should comply with Congress. But to your question: Say they don’t respond to the voluntary letter for records or testimony. There’s an impasse; then the committee would issue a subpoena. At that point the administration would have to basically defy a subpoena, have some sort of reason for doing that based on a constitutional privilege, like executive privilege. If the committee doesn’t buy that argument, the committee can choose to hold the president in contempt and then go to the floor of either the House or Senate for that contempt vote. Now, at the floor there are two options. And you’re talking about the first one, which is criminal contempt. Criminal contempt is a statutory provision. It says: DOJ shall present the criminal contempt from Congress to a grand jury. And that statute was passed in the 1800s. It was used for decades without any challenges by the executive branch. The U.S. attorneys would dutifully present these criminal-contempt citations to the grand juries and process them. That continued until about the 1980s. And in the 1980s, it was during the Gorsuch investigation that the House was conducting, where the DOJ said, We don’t think “shall” means “shall” in the statute. In other words, prosecutors have to have discretion to decide whether or not to go forward on a case. And the traditional idea of this is: Prosecutorial discretion’s on the merits. So for example, in my old committee, the House Oversight Committee, we were investigating the IRS’s alleged targeting of conservative groups, and Lois Lerner was the official who came to testify. She took the Fifth, but then she kind of kept talking during her opening statement, so the committee concluded she had waived her Fifth Amendment. It got referred over to Department of Justice, and the prosecutors thought, You know, it’s too close a case. I don’t think we’re going to win this on merits. We’re not going to go forward. So that was prosecutorial discretion. The second point DOJ made was: If a president asserts executive privilege over certain information, DOJ is not going to prosecute an executive-branch official over which executive privilege has been asserted in terms of the records or testimony at issue. So that decision by DOJ removed criminal prosecution in those two areas: either prosecutorial discretion on the merits or in cases of executive privilege. Since then, it’s evolved into a free-for-all, basically, under the Trump administration. Now, it doesn’t matter whether it’s prosecutorial discretion; doesn’t matter if it’s executive privilege. DOJ can just refuse to prosecute for any reason. So I think under the next two years, as far as criminal contempt is concerned, it’s not really a viable option. Frum: Let’s start with a realistic scenario. So the Department of Defense—or the Department of War as it now styles itself, but the Department of Defense as it’s known in law—has granted a number of contracts to companies in which the president’s children have had interests. And so one of the questions that a new Congress might be interested in is: Were these contracts handled in an arm’s-length manner? Or was there some special favoritism or influence on behalf of the president’s children with the contracts? So Congress will say, We will go to the companies and DoD, and say, “We want more information about these contracts.” Play that scenario out. How does that game go? Rapallo: Yeah, and we conducted a pretty similar investigation after the Iraq War during the reconstruction-contracting issues that were happening with the Pentagon. Yeah—basically from a committee’s point of view, you’re going to make requests to all the parties, right? You’re going to make requests to the Pentagon, to the private contractors, to anyone else involved, and collect information from all of the sources. In this case, there wouldn’t be really an executive privilege. This isn’t talking about close advisers to the president giving him advice. If it did come into that, you could make an assertion there. But the rest of the information we received, in terms of contracts, we received reports from auditors. All the information that you’d expect to get in a congressional investigation we were able to receive. Now, I don’t know under the current presidency whether they’ll comply with those requests. They might have an interest in just dragging this out: forcing Congress to go to court and litigate this in civil court, maybe. But I don’t think that’s going to be uniform in terms of all the people receiving the inquiries from Congress, all the people receiving subpoenas. Frum: So the companies, for example, might say: You know what? We got the contracts in the first place. But we have an eye to the future here. The company will be in business after 2029, and we think it might be in our interest to actually disclose to Congress what it wants to know. Rapallo: Absolutely. And they also know that it’s completely legal and within Congress’s oversight responsibility. And so it’s going to be a loser, I think, in court, if it goes to that. And just like you say, they want to continue working for the government after the next two years are over. They also might be a publicly traded company and have to report some of these things to their shareholders, which also may factor into their decision. Frum: So President Trump, in the famous Mazars case, went to court to argue: I, as a president, or ex-president in that case, can block the companies I deal with from sharing information with Congress that I don’t want them to share. How is your assessment of that kind of Mazars—if we can call it that—kind of Mazars strategy? How does that look today? Rapallo: Yeah, that was an interesting case. Because—and I worked on that case—as the committee, we were actually trying to be mindful of what the court said to get information from other sources. So we went to the outside accounting firms to get information. What President Trump did in that case is, he sued Mazars— Frum: The accounting firm— Rapallo: Yes, exactly. To block them. And then the House intervened in that litigation in order to represent the House’s interests. So, I think using proactive litigation like that is definitely one of the tools the president has shown that he’s willing to use, and he could try it again. Frum: How much of this is a legal game, and how much is a political game? And let me give you another real-world example. So President Trump made his first post-reelection fortune by selling a memecoin. And he made a lot of money from the memecoin. The memecoin promptly fell to worthlessness, and many people lost their investment. Some of those people probably knew that this was just a way of giving money to the president and aren’t mad that they lost their investment. But some of the people may have been genuinely duped and may be mad. If you subpoena those people, what happens? Would the president try to stop them? And is simply telling their story all that Congress needs? It doesn’t need further legal remedy; it just needs the world to see that President Trump pocketed a lot of money from a transaction in which other people are enormous losers. Rapallo: Yeah, I think it’s both a legal and a political issue in that case. From the legal side, there’s no doubt that Congress has a right to collect information, testimony, from anybody that it wants to in order to help inform the legislative process. And so it can definitely have those people come in, testify. It’s a pretty routine thing for committees to have victims come in and have a hearing just devoted to hearing them out. Hearing what their concerns are. So that wouldn’t be out of the ordinary at all. People would probably want to hear that. Frum: Now, many of the people that Congress will want to learn more about, like, Corey Lewandowski at Homeland Security, who was apparently trying to intervene in government contracts. He was a special government employee. I think Steve Witkoff, the president’s envoy, whose family has been doing business in the region to which he’s a special envoy, both Russia and the Middle East. What is the standing—if Congress wants to find out more about the business dealings of special government employees while they were doing whatever they were doing for government, how does that work? And are there limits? Or do you have more range with a special government employee? Rapallo: I don’t think that the fact that they’re a special government employee makes a difference to the committees. The committees can get information from private individuals, special government employees, regular government employees, contractors: anybody. It’s up to Congress to determine what information it needs to do its job. What might come into play is there was this—and you may be referencing this—there was the Justice Department opinion over the summer that purported to say that executive privilege could apply to people outside the government. And that was new. That hadn’t happened before. Normally DOJ only issues those kinds of opinions if they relate to a specific case or controversy or something that they’re dealing with. That one didn’t. That one didn’t have anything to do with a specific case at all. So to me, that was a tell, I think, that they think—at least they thought during the summer—that they have a very good chance of losing the House or Senate, and they were trying to get ahead of it. Frum: Let me invite you to step onto the other side of the game for a moment—the president’s side. Some of the scandals, or some of the alleged scandals, in the Trump world don’t seem to involve the president or his family personally. So there’s a big—right now there’s a lot of reporting about money that flowed in and out of the Kennedy Center. There are accusations that some millions of dollars of that money have disappeared, and that’s acrimony between people who are in Trump’s orbit. But Trump himself doesn’t seem, at least at this point, to have received any benefit or any alleged benefit from these alleged transactions. If you’re advising President Trump—and now think of this from that point of view, not the West Wing president, but the actual President Trump—do you say, You know what? Throw Congress some bones here. There are people you can sacrifice ? Or do you need to defend everybody, because if any one of them talks, it could bring down the whole house of cards? Rapallo: It’s really hard for me to get inside his head, just in terms of trying to predict what he’s done in the past. I’ve not been a great predictor of it. But, it’s really hard, because he has shown times where he would do both, right? He’s shown times where—I mean, this recent case where they called on the ambassador to Greece to resign. They were willing to do that. But in other cases, it’s been a blanket refusal—like during impeachment—a blanket refusal. No agencies will cooperate with this whatsoever. I could see arguments going either way. I could see some people advising him, You know what? You’ve got two years. You can drag this out. You can wait it out. You can go to court. You can embrace civil litigation, to just go that route. But I think the counter to that is all of the other people in the Republican Party who are going to be facing reelection in 2028, including some people in his Cabinet potentially. If, in that case, if a committee sent a letter to Secretary of State about this ambassador to Greece, he might have a very different response to Congress than President Trump would, right? If he thinks he’s running for president, he might want to do something where it’s a little more forthcoming. Frum: Let me ask you about something you said about the two-year deadline. Is that really the case? Because this present political dispensation may not be over in two years. Let me give you an example of what I have in mind. So, there’s this plane that the United States Department of Defense has received on a temporary basis from the government of Qatar. And the terms of the gift, as I understand them, are: It’s to be used by the United States to fly the president around for two years, then it’s to go to the presidential library, whatever the presidential library is. And maybe the engine is taken out, like the plane in the Reagan Library. Or maybe it’s just, you know, a library asset that’s available for other members of the family to use who are on the board—board members of the library, or the former president himself if he’s on the board of his own library. So that may be an ongoing matter. The Constitution says you can’t accept any gifts without the explicit approval of Congress, and I don’t know whether that would apply differently after the president leaves office than it applies before he leaves office. How does that story work itself out? Rapallo: Yeah. Well, to your basic point, I think you’re right. That’s sort of the point I was trying to make with the Marco Rubio example—that this will go beyond the two-year period, even though some advisers might be telling him, You can wait this out for two years. There are going to be implications well past those two years. On that particular case, it just seems like such an egregious and obvious example of a violation of the emoluments clause. He doesn’t have consent from Congress to do that. The question is, what can Congress do about it? And I know [Representative] Jamie Raskin has some legislation to kind of put some teeth into the constitutional provision to have a remedy, but the current Congress hasn’t shown any willingness to go forward on that. So it really will depend on what the makeup of the new Congress looks like. Frum: How much time does Congress have? I mean, one of the defenses that the Trump people might have inadvertently put up is if you—let’s say you have hundreds of scandals, that many of them must necessarily go by the board. Because Congress doesn’t have the resources; doesn’t have the time. Is that a kind of defense? Can you simply give Congress information in some cases of the least damaging stuff? Flood the zone with lots of information about the least damaging stuff, and then play for time with the more damaging stuff—and just count on Congress’s desire for easy and early wins to protect the president from more dangerous lines of inquiry? Rapallo: It’s an interesting strategy. Definitely—papering a committee with useless information is an old trick that a lot of agencies have used in the past. I think it’s going to be up to Congress to triage. I think you’re exactly right. There are so many scandals. I mean, I felt this way in the first Trump administration: that there were so many things to focus on. We had to triage; we had to coordinate with other committees to make sure that they were covering things that were different, we weren’t having overlap duplication, that sort of thing. I think they’re going to have to do that even more this time around, because there are so many just blatant examples of violating statutes that Congress has passed. Reallocating funding to purposes Congress never approved. All of these things that you’re mentioning. So triage is going to be really important. Frum: Well, we say Congress as if it’s a thing, but there are two houses of Congress that often have unharmonious relationships. Within those two branches, there are many committees whose chairs have egos and agendas, and they don’t always get along. Even if Congress has more time than I just suggested, there’s certainly not infinite attention from the media, which is what members of the Congress are seeking. So can triaging work? Or do you just get train wrecks as chairs of committee battle each other for attention, for authority, for money? Rapallo: I think triage can work if there’s coordination. Congress is like hundreds of different stovepipes coming out with each individual office member, each committee office, each leadership office. And so there really has to be coordination in the committees and across committees, and ideally across the Hill if both houses flip. Frum: Who does the coordination? Rapallo: Yeah, that’s the problem. So it’s got to be— Frum: Who’s in charge of that? Rapallo: It’s got to be leadership. It can be member-driven. I’ve seen both iterations of it. If you have two committees on either side, sister committees on the House and Senate being able to work together, that can be effective as well. But it does require some leadership in terms of just de-duplicating, right? You don’t want everybody focusing on one shiny object as it continues to change. Frum: Well, depending on the numbers of new members elected, and who they are, the next Congress may start off with a leadership battle in both House and Senate. And that consumes a lot of time and builds a lot of acrimony and gets in the way of coordination. I mean, if Leader [Senator Chuck] Schumer keeps his job, but only after he’s had a lot of dissent from the left of the party, if there’s a challenge to [Representative] Hakeem Jeffries, how do you coordinate after that kind of fratricidal battle? Rapallo: I thankfully came up under Speaker [Nancy] Pelosi, and she was very effective at sort of fending these things off. I think they do happen. Obviously, they’ve happened on the Republican side, and they do pose challenges in terms of time organizing different factions, that sort of thing. I think it’s just part of the system. You just have to go through that process, get through the other side, and figure out where you are. That doesn’t mean that committees can’t be planning and talking to each other and organizing while that’s all happening. You know, the chairs of the committees are probably pretty set, although there might be a few outliers. But during that same period, from November to January, it’s very dramatic in particular in the House, because the ratio of staff and budget is two to one, majority to minority. It’s a little different than the Senate. So when it flips, it’s really dramatic. The majority will let about half of their staff go. The minority will have to staff up in about two months, doubling their staff, while they’re also figuring out what topics they want to focus on, while they’re also moving offices, changing furniture, computers, the whole thing. So they really are—and they’re used to this—building the plane while they fly it. Frum: Is there the depth of talent in the Democratic world to do that kind of staffing and to get the right kind of people who can do this? Well, it sounds like it’s going to be pretty laborious, forensic, number-crunching, legal-crunching to get to the bottom of allegation after allegation after allegation. Rapallo: Yeah. I think you do have some really talented people. I think there are a lot of folks who are Democrats who used to be in the government, or used to be on the Hill, who are very interested in coming back. I would be completely surprised if the Democrats in the House and Senate weren’t at least having coffees with people to figure out who they were going to bring on, what expertise they need, and how they were going to structure their internal staff should things change over. Frum: Compare and contrast the Senate and the House as investigative bodies. I think many of us have memories that some of the most sober investigations in American history were done by the Senate rather than by the House, but not in every case. What are the advantages, what are the disadvantages that each of those bodies has if there’s a Democratic majority in one or the other to do the investigation? Rapallo: So I’m a House guy; I should just say that. I’ve never worked in the Senate. But from my perch on the House side, it seems like the Senate has much more power in terms of actual tools that they can use. We talk about how difficult it is without criminal contempt and being stuck in civil court for a long time, but the Senate’s got a lot of other tools that they can use. You know—they can hold up nominees, they can filibuster bills or just hold them if they’re in the majority at this point. But they have tools that they can use to extract concessions to get information. And there’ve been plenty of examples of that happening in the past, where they’re using their tools not just because they might oppose certain legislation, but because they’re trying to get information out of the administration. Now, with that said, my impression on the House side is that the Senate can be a lot slower, just in terms of being able to call a hearing or being able to conduct an investigation. The one body that is sort of their chief investigative body—the PSI, Permanent Subcommittee on Investigation—they do fantastic work. They have excellent people. Traditionally, they focused on primarily bipartisan investigations that are very in-depth, that may go more than a year or two. And they, at the end of that process, come out with a really hefty, meaty report and a hearing. My experience on the House side is that it’s sometimes preferable to be much more agile and dynamic and be able to call a hearing very quickly—in order to get information and keep the drumbeat going in terms of getting even more information down the line. Frum: You talked about the ratio of staff in House and Senate. Is there some objective limit on staff? Could the House say, You know what? This is a hornets’ nest that we’ve never seen before. We’re going to need 1,000 more investigators than we’ve ever employed before, and we want to employ 1,000 more investigators. Could they do that? Rapallo: Well, not only could they do that, but right now the House and Senate are so far below their historic levels. They’re way below what they used to be in the ’70s and ’80s, and I think that happened at least on the House side in the [Newt] Gingrich era. He came in, and staff was drastically, drastically reduced to the point where there’s a lot of commentators who talk about not even being up to the level it used to be. How in the world is Congress supposed to be able to conduct oversight over this massive growing bureaucracy, with all of these different agencies, when they don’t even have the same level of staff they used to? I think there’s a really strong argument for not just going back to at least those levels, but for increasing significantly. And I think it should be a long-term bipartisan effort, not just related to the current circumstances we find ourselves in with President Trump. Frum: I’m going to ask what may be a tactless question you will answer tactfully. You, as a longtime staff director—how do you communicate to the chairman of a committee or the chairwoman of a committee, You know, we’d get better answers if you talked less and let the staff do the questioning ? Rapallo: ( Laughs .) Frum: How does that conversation go? Rapallo: I’m not sure I would ever say that to my boss. ( Laughs .) But I had fantastic bosses. I mean, I worked for Henry Waxman, who was a pro, and I worked for Elijah Cummings, who was just fantastic. Frum: Okay, let’s say it never, ever happened to you. But there are surely staff directors of whom it’s true that it would be better if the committee let the counsel ask the questions and the people in the big chairs kept quiet. How can that be done? Or is it just hopeless? They’re going to talk, and nothing can be done about it. Rapallo: So, where this tends to come up a little more than, like, in a public hearing would be in a deposition, right? So depositions are held in private. They’re usually conducted by counsel. But members can come, and sometimes they do, and sometimes they want to ask a lot of questions. Sometimes those questions aren’t exactly on point. You know, it’s something—they just walked in the room, they had heard outside, something like that. The best tactic, I think, from a staff perspective, is to be able to explain to the members all the work that’s gone into prepping for that deposition, and how you’ve got, you know, 10 lines of questions you want to make sure that you get through. And if the member does want to come in, it would be fantastic if the member could focus on this particular line. And by the way, why don’t we go outside and we can talk you through it? We can walk through the elements of it, ideally beforehand, before the member comes in. Frum: Well, in a deposition, there’s no TV camera, so I assume that’s an easier conversation. But in a room where there is a TV camera, it’s a tougher conversation. Rapallo: Yeah; I think our practice on the oversight committee was to staff the members, was to give them the best staffing they could have. We would work on question lines into the night to make sure that they were not only well thought out, but they had key evidence, prepping exhibits, that sort of thing, so that each member would be ready. And that developed—it started during the Waxman period, and it continued to develop, and it really paid off, because the members started to see the value in having those well-thought-through question lines. Frum: President Trump, there’s a story, there’s a report out—I don’t know how valid, but it sounds right—that President Trump is considering massive in-advance pardons of maybe hundreds, maybe dozens, maybe hundreds of people as a way of immunizing them against being subpoenaed, or being asked to testify, or being held to any kind of account for things that have been done that were wrong. How does that pardon power intersect with the subpoena power? Rapallo: Sure. So the pardon power pardons a crime, right? Or a potential crime. It prevents any later prosecution of the act that’s pardoned. It doesn’t prevent somebody from being subpoenaed to testify about information that they know. So, any witness who’s pardoned would still have an obligation to comply with a congressional subpoena to come up and testify. Frum: It protects them from punishment if they defy a subpoena. Rapallo: It can only do that if the act has occurred. It can’t pardon a future crime. So, at the end—say, what I think you’re getting at is, say somebody refuses to testify. At the end of the Trump administration, that’s where the pardon could come. There couldn’t be any later prosecution of that act. But there’s nothing to prevent the next Congress from recalling that person and asking them to testify again, sort of like the January 6th committee did. A subsequent administration brings people in, and there can’t be a future pardon for that act. Frum: So that suggests that the pardon is a less potent tool of stonewalling than it seems. But is that a comfort, or is that a realistic theory, or is it actually a more potent tool than that nice summary suggests? Think like a stonewaller for a minute. Rapallo: I think it will give people comfort if their idea is to stonewall for this two-year period. I don’t think it will protect people after that two-year period. But then maybe they roll the dice and think, The dynamic will be different then, and maybe Congress loses interest in me . Or something like that. Frum: All right. Now let me ask you a question taking us beyond 2028 and 2029. So let’s say there are—not everyone has been pardoned, and there are lines of questioning, and there has been stonewalling, and there are subpoenas that have been defied, and there’s a new president, a non-Trump-protective president in 2029. Maybe even a Republican non-Trump-protective president. How much of its energy, its mandate, will a new administration want to give to resolving these matters from the past? Is there a risk that, as I think happened in the Biden administration, the president says: You know what? Let’s just let bygones be bygones. I’ve got things I want to do. History can take care of itself ? Rapallo: Yeah, I think there’s always going to be that discussion. And it’ll happen with the members as well, members of the House and Senate. Do we want to look backwards? Do we want to look forward? And I think a lot of that will depend on the dynamics of policy. Like, Could we actually now use our majorities and a like-minded president to get some of our policies into effect? If that’s the case, there’s going to be less focus on the past. However, given the really unprecedented nature of the Trump presidency, one of those policy goals might be a complete reset on accountability, right? And passing laws that can re-reestablish some of the safeguards that norms were doing the heavy work for before. So that could be one of the policy agenda items going forward. And as part of that, you may want to include or continue investigations into those topics. Frum: Do you have a view on whether we need institutional or even constitutional reform? Some way to make the Department of Justice more independent of the executive of the moment? Some constraint on the pardon power to make sure it’s not used corruptly? Or is that just idle speculation and beyond the realm of real-world politics? Rapallo: Well, it’s—yes, I do. I think the previous notion of DOJ being semi-independent had always been taken seriously, and now I think that’s basically gone. Can a future president restore it? I’m sure that some will want to try, but now the damage is done, right? You know it can happen again. Or can you impose some safeguards? I’m not confident with the current Supreme Court, that they would sort of allow true independence. I think Congress would have to work through all the details of the U.S.-versus-Trump case, and all the cases involving the appointment power and that sort of thing. But I do think Congress could make a change. David Frum: Because I want to test a theory, and you tell me what you think of this. So in the 1970s, we saw a big expansion of the regulatory state and the creation of a lot of new kinds of regulatory bodies, and big delegations of power from Congress to the president from everything from the environment to civil rights to trade policy. But Congress in the 1970s said, But we have a safety belt here, which is: If we’ve got a provision in this law that if these delegated powers, the powers we’re giving to the president, are abused in any way that we don’t like, we can veto it. And Congress can say, No, no, not that. Don’t issue that regulation. Don’t take this action. You, your delegate, we can withdraw the power that we have delegated. And the Supreme Court in the 1980s said that that congressional veto is unconstitutional—Congress can’t do that. But the delegations did not get voided. Congress delegated a lot of power thinking it had a safety belt, and the safety belt is taken away, and the delegations are all still there. And these bodies are all supposed to work in ways that—but they were all premised on a mechanism that no longer exists. And we’re kind of in the ruins of that system. And maybe it’s all unfixable without finding some way to either get the congressional veto back, or withdrawing the delegations that were premised on the congressional veto. And forgive me if that was unclear to anybody who’s listening or watching. Rapallo: No, you’re absolutely correct. You described that really well. In fact, I have a colleague here at Georgetown Law, Josh Chafetz, who’s written an article about this exact topic, pointing out that the Supreme Court in one of the cases was Chadha . This is—“ The Chadha Presidency ” is the title of his article, because the veto power was taken away, but all of the grants of authority the court let stand. And not only that, in order to take those back, Congress would have to pass a new law that would have to overcome a presidential veto—which wouldn’t have been the case if they had just invalidated the entire law. So it’s actually harder to repeal the delegations than it would’ve been otherwise. So you’re exactly right the way you described that. Frum: Any brainwaves as to what’s the exit from this box of delegation, without a safety belt? Rapallo: Well, I think the appropriations power has got to be the linchpin to that. It’s a core congressional power. There have been a lot of discussions about how to use that power more effectively. Part of it also will be staffing up in Congress: increasing staffing levels so that the staffers have the expertise instead of delegating a lot of this to the agencies under the Chevron -type doctrines. But I think the key, from my perspective as a congressional investigator, is information. Access to information. I mean, without information you’re legislating in the dark. You can’t adequately monitor current programs. You can’t do all of the functions that the Constitution requires Congress to do in an informed way. And the Supreme Court has said this over and over again, that each house is supposed to have its own independent power to demand information and then compel that information. And that, to me, is one key thing that’s really atrophied over the last several decades. Frum: Well, so let’s end our conversation on a hopeful note, for any young lawyers listening. If you’re worried that AI is going to devour your job in document review or contract approval or anything like that, the Congress is going to be hiring very large numbers, it sounds like, of legally qualified people. So there is a job for you that looks likely to survive the AI revolution, at least for the next two years and maybe beyond. Rapallo: Exactly. Yeah, I think there will be a lot of hires if you’re—and also it’s just a fantastic place to work. You know, as a lawyer, sometimes you might represent an individual, which can be critically, critically important. Could be a life-or-death matter. But for Congress, you get the chance to really think about the interest of millions, if not hundreds of millions, of people. Frum: Thank you, Dave. Thank you so much for making time. I know how in demand you are, and I know how much more in demand you’re likely to be in the coming weeks. So I’m glad we got in under your wire. Thank you so much for joining me on The David Frum Show today. Rapallo: Thank you for having me. Frum: Bye-bye. [ Music ] Frum: Thanks so much to Dave Rapallo for joining me today on The David Frum Show . As I said at the top of the show, this week’s book is I, Robot by Isaac Asimov. I need to make clear here—I, these days, am not a big consumer of science fiction. I read a lot of it as a boy, but that’s not why I return to it now. I return to it now because it’s becoming kind of obvious to me that just about everybody with a major view on the looming AI debate that is going to matter so much in the next Congress has had a lot of their views about the AI revolution formed by a combination of Isaac Asimov and Ayn Rand. Ayn Rand we’ll save for another day; Isaac Asimov for today. I, Robot was published in 1950. But it’s a collection of short stories, not a novel: a collection of short stories that Asimov published in his 20s between 1940 and 1950. Now Isaac Asimov, if you’ve not heard of him, was a kind of prodigy. He became one of the world’s influential and famous writers still in his 20s. He’s a clever writer, an ingenious writer, kind of an attractive writer. He had a kinda technological optimism. He was also—I don’t mean this in a disrespectful way—but he was a kind of shallow writer. He had a very limited emotional range. I think there was something missing from his makeup, that he had a few emotions—but the full range of human experience, he never really entered into that. And that was both his strength and his weakness. The stories in I, Robot describe a series of situations in which human beings find themselves interacting in the future with highly capable robots. Often quite human, human-looking robots. And along the way, Asimov coins a series of rules that he calls Asimov’s —or some people have called— Asimov’s three laws of robotics . Asimov always gave credit to the editor of the science-fiction magazine in which he published the stories for actually formalizing the rules, but the rules are attributed to him, and it doesn’t matter who the ultimate origin is. They’re in his stories. And here are his three rules. And if you’re a science-fiction fan, you probably know them by heart. The first rule was: A robot may not injure a human being, or through inaction allow a human being to come to harm. Second: A robot must obey orders given by human beings, except where such orders conflict with the first law. And the third rule: A robot must protect its own existence, so long as that does not conflict with the first or second law. Now, these three rules, or three laws it should be said, are not laws in the sense of some kind of worked-out code. They’re dramatic devices, because actually they can’t all be reconciled. And the interest of the short stories in the I, Robot collection comes from watching the conflict and impossibility of these three rules work themselves out. But I keep getting the feeling that there are people who have enormous power over all our lives who regard I, Robot as a kind of like the Bible or Book of Mormon or Quran, or something that they can actually deduce real life, real-world life by, and live by. And not only live for themselves, but live for the rest of us. So it needs to be stressed that you should go back and read these things to understand that the whole point to the three laws in the short stories is that they don’t work. They lead to constant surprises. Now, because Asimov is a basically optimistic person and, again, kind of a shallow person with a limited range, the conflicts and the consequences of these rules not working is never too terrible in the short stories. But the book that he set himself to refuse, to write against, the book that’s looming in the background of all of these short stories, which is Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein . That book—which is the real book for our age, the real inspiration—that book reminds us the happy endings promised by Isaac Asimov are not necessarily the truth, and are not necessarily the conclusion we’d come to if we thought deeply about the era into which we are moving. That’s it for this week’s David Frum Show. Thanks so much for joining me today, for watching, and for listening. As always, the best way to support the work of this program, if you’re minded, and to support all of us at The Atlantic, is by subscribing to The Atlantic. I hope you will consider doing that. See you soon here on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.

items.title: CHU de Pala : Un volumineux myome utérin de 5,865 grammes retiré avec succès chez une patiente de 30 ans
items.description: Le Service de Gynécologie-Obstétrique et de Médecine de la Reproduction (SGOMR) du Centre hospitalier universitaire de Pala (CHU-P) a réalisé avec succès une intervention chirurgicale majeure sur une patiente de 30 ans présentant un désir de grossesse. L’intervention, réalisée par laparotomie, a permis l’ablation d’un volumineux myome utérin pesant 5 865 grammes. Au cours de cette opération, l’équipe chirurgicale a également procédé à une adhésiolyse visant à libérer les nombreuses adhérences pelviennes, ainsi qu’à une plastie tubaire bilatérale. Ces gestes chirurgicaux avaient pour objectif d’améliorer les conditions anatomiques et de préserver les possibilités de conception de la patiente. L’intervention a mobilisé l’équipe chirurgicale conduite par le Dr GUIRO Noura, DES en médecine de la reproduction et attachés en chirurgie ainsi que l’équipe d’anesthésiste conduite par le Dr SAWADOGO Arouna, DES en anesthésie réanimation. Cette intervention illustre les compétences techniques et l’engagement des équipes du SGOMR dans la prise en charge des pathologies gynécologiques complexes et l’accompagnement des femmes ayant un désir de maternité. À travers ces avancées, le CHU-P réaffirme sa volonté de développer une offre de soins spécialisée et de contribuer à l’amélioration de la santé reproductive des femmes. Service de communication
